stories.bodyText:

The Supreme Court is set to pronounce its judgment today (November 20, 2026) on an application filed by Tamil Nadu in the decades-old Cauvery water-sharing dispute. The State has contended that there is a shortfall of 11.719 thousand million cubic feet (tmcft) in the flows due to it at Billigundulu, the inter-State border measuring point, up to October 6.
Also read | Tamil Nadu’s claim of Cauvery backlog and the Supreme Court’s response | Explained
The State has also accused Karnataka of withholding water despite having sufficient reserves, pointing to a combined reservoir storage of approximately 49 tmcft, which it maintained was adequate to meet its water-sharing obligations to the lower riparian State.
Earlier, Karnataka, in an affidavit filed before the Supreme Court, had argued that Tamil Nadu had been allocated the lion’s share of 404.25 tmcft on account of its historic irrigation claims, while Karnataka received only 284.75 tmcft out of the 483 tmcft available up to Billigundulu, without adequately accounting for its drought-prone areas.

stories.headline: Video of Bihar CM’s security ‘pushing’ Nishant sparks row
stories.deck: Alliance partner Janata Dal (United) objected strongly, saying the Assembly mandate was in Nitish Kumar’s name. The party demanded action, calling it an insult to Nishant and all its workers
stories.bodyText:
A row erupted in Bihar on Thursday (November 19, 2026) after a video went viral on social media purportedly showing a security officer of Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary ‘pushing’ State Health Minister Nishant Kumar.
The incident took place in Vaishali district on Wednesday (November 18, 2026) when both leaders went to inspect the venue that Prime Minister Narendra Modi is scheduled to visit on November 21 to inaugurate a six-lane bridge named after Mr. Nishant’s father and former Chief Minister Nitish Kumar.
JD(U) seeks probe
Janata Dal (United) [JD(U)] MLC and chief spokesperson Neeraj Kumar raised a strong objection over the incident and demanded that the Bihar police investigate the matter and find out whether it was done intentionally or inadvertently. He also termed the video “disturbing and painful”.
“Nishant Kumar is the Minister in-charge of Vaishali district and had gone with the Chief Minister,” Mr. Neeraj told reporters at his official residence in Patna.
The Opposition Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) also took a dig at the National Democratic Alliance (NDA) government by sharing the video on X. “As soon as poor Nitish Kumar fell ill and became unconscious, the BJP first snatched his Chief Minister’s post. Now, poor Nitish is having his son pushed around by the BJP’s CM police officers,” the RJD said.
RJD Chief Lalu Prasad’s daughter, Rohini Acharya, also posted the video on X and asked, “Why are Uncle Nitish Kumar and brother Nishant Kumar being forced to endure humiliation?”
“First, Nitish Kumar was sidelined in a humiliating manner, and now the BJP is publicly humiliating his son Nishant. It seems Nitish ji has completely buried his self-respect and dignity, and now he is forcing his son to fall in line with his own ways too,” Ms. Acharya wrote in the post
Asked about any possibility of the RJD and the JD(U) coming together once again, Leader of the Opposition and RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav said, “I do now know what people are talking about, but whatever I had said before the election, everything is coming true. I had said the BJP will not allow Nitishji to remain in the CM’s post, it has happened.”
He further said, “JD(U) is no longer united; it has become divided. For their own vested interests and comfort, Sanjay Jha and Lalan Singh took Nitish Ji to the BJP. They want to finish JD(U); that’s why Nishant is not made Deputy Chief Minister. Forget Deputy CM—if Nitish Ji were CM, Nishant would also have been made CM. If Nitish Ji were in a conscious state, he would have been in Mahagathbandhan.”
A few days ago, RJD MP from Aurangabad, Abhay Kushwaha, said that Lalu Prasad and Tejashwi would welcome Nitish if he wishes to return to the Mahagathbandhan. Mr. Kushwaha went on to say that if Nitish wishes, his son could be made Chief Minister.
‘Human error’
The Special Security Group tasked with the protection of the CM conducted a probe and termed the incident ‘human error’.

stories.headline: Earth gains a new companion — a mini moon — but won't stick around for long
stories.bodyText:
Earth gains a new companion — a mini moon — but won't stick around for long
It's a tiny space rock that will be orbiting around Earth temporarily until December 2026 or January next year, continuing its journey in the solar system.
Earth has captured a new mini moon. It's a tiny space rock that will be orbiting around the planet temporarily until December 2026 or January next year, continuing its journey in the solar system.
The object named 2026 QQ8 was discovered by astronomer Krisztin Srneczky on August 20, 2026, according to the International Astronomical Union's (IAU) Minor Planet Center (MPC).
A mini moon is a small asteroid temporarily captured by Earth's gravity, resulting in a short-term orbit around the planet.
The observations made using the University of Hawaii 2.2-meter telescope and the Lowell Discovery Telescope led astronomers to confirm that 2026 QQ8 is not a piece of human-made space debris.
Following this, the MPC confirmed that 2026 QQ8 is natural in origin and is likely a small asteroid.
This mini moon is classified as an Aten asteroid, a group of asteroids that are near-Earth asteroids, cross occasionally into our planet’s orbit, and orbit closer to the Sun than our planet does.
It was captured by Earth's gravity in April 2026 when it passed close to Earth's Hill sphere, the region where Earth's gravitational pull dominated over the Sun's.
Its trajectory, or the path around Earth, is an irregular loop rather than a neat circle.
Remarkably, this is not the first time this asteroid has crossed Earth’s orbit. It crosses Earth's orbit around once every 10 years.
Earth had temporarily captured mini moons previously. They include 2020 SO, 2020 CD3, and 2024 PT5. Our planet also has quasi-moons, such as 2025 PN7, which appears to orbit our planet but actually orbits the Sun, sharing a similar orbital period to Earth's.

stories.headline: Bengaluru man finds expired chocolates in Blinkit gift pack, gets Rs 43,479 compensation
stories.deck: A 30-year-old man's Valentine's Day chocolate order from Blinkit contained expired items, causing a complaint. The Bangalore Urban IV Additional District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission held Blinkit responsible for deficiency in service. Despite their defense, the commission found it unacceptable to deliver expired products to customers. As a result, Blinkit was ordered to refund the…
stories.bodyText:
BENGALURU: The chocolates tasted off, and when a 30-year-old finally read the wrappers, he understood why. Half the gift box he had ordered for Valentine's Day had expired two months before it reached his doorstep. Now, quick-commerce platform Blinkit must pay far more than the Rs 479 he spent after the Bangalore Urban IV Additional District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission held it guilty of deficiency in service and unfair trade practice.
The saga began on February 14, 2026, when Manju Prasad K, a resident of Hegganahalli Cross, ordered a Choco Cart Chocolate Gift Pack (Grand) through the Blinkit app. He paid Rs 479 through UPI, comprising Rs 469 for the product and Rs 10 in handling charges. The pack, weighing 223.5 grams and containing six varieties of chocolates, arrived in about 20 minutes.
Over the next five days, he ate the chocolates. On February 21, he noticed a change in their taste and checked the individual wrappers. He found that three of the six chocolates had expired on December 14, 2025, while the other three were close to their expiry dates.
He immediately complained to Blinkit's help desk and followed up with an email on February 28. 
The company replied that complaints had to be raised within seven days of delivery and that it could not process a refund or replacement. Prasad approached the commission on March 23, seeking a refund of Rs 479, compensation of Rs 25 lakh and Rs 15,000 towards litigation and travel expenses.
In their defence, Blinkit and Blink Commerce Pvt Ltd argued that the product page carried a return policy allowing replacements only within 72 hours of delivery and that the complaint had been filed after this period. They also contended that his consumption of the chocolates over five days had deprived them of an opportunity to verify the product. Further, they argued that the expiry dates on individual wrappers did not establish that the entire pack was expired or unfit for consumption. Pointing to the absence of medical records, prescriptions or bills, they said no injury had been demonstrated and sought dismissal of the complaint with exemplary costs.
The commission noted that the companies had cited both a seven-day and a 72-hour limit, positions it found contradictory. It observed that the box had been delivered at around 11.45 pm, making it impossible for the complainant to consume all six varieties on the same day. It therefore held that the February 21 complaint was filed within seven days of delivery. It also pointed out that the original wrappers had been produced before it and that the companies had not specifically denied supplying expired chocolates, but had primarily disputed the complaint on the ground of delay.
The commission observed: “It is not the question of replacement of the chocolate box or refund of the amount, as a seller should not keep expired edible things in the shop.” It described the practice of packing good and expired chocolates in the same gift box as “highly condemnable”. It also accepted Prasad's argument that this was done around Christmas and Valentine's Day, when buyers might not check the expiry dates. The commission noted that Blinkit's counsel had not objected to this submission.
Calling it a matter of public health, the commission said many people in cities such as Bengaluru depended on online platforms and that taking advantage of their trust was unfair.
Holding that the companies had supplied expired chocolates despite knowing that they had expired two months before delivery, the commission found them guilty of deficiency in service and unfair trade practice. The bench, comprising president Vijaykumar M Pawale, member Chandrashekar S Noola and lady member K Anita Shivakumar, partly allowed the complaint on November 6.
In the order authored by K Anita Shivakumar, the commission directed both companies to jointly refund Rs 479 and pay Rs 3,000 as compensation for mental agony and hardship. It also imposed punitive damages of Rs 40,000 under Section 39(1)(g) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, to be remitted to the Consumer Welfare Fund.

briefs.headline: In a first, Japanese forces will use Indian facilities for live-fire training
briefs.deck: Foreign and Defence Ministers of the two countries hold talks in Tokyo; both sides announce deepening security and defence cooperation in joint statement, indicate forward movement in India receiving the UNICORN naval radar system from Japan
briefs.bodyText:
India and Japan on Thursday (November 19, 2026) held a “two-plus-two” Foreign and Defence Ministers’ dialogue in Tokyo, where the two sides welcomed the signing of a Letter of Intent (LoI) that will, for the first time, allow Japan’s Self-Defence Forces to use Indian test ranges for “live-fire training..., including those involving surface-to-ship missiles”.
The two sides also indicated forward movement towards India receiving the Unified Complex Radio Antenna, or UNICORN, naval radar system from Japan, and discussed the ongoing revisions in Japan’s national security and defence policies.
“They welcomed the signing of LOI toward the utilisation of firing ranges in India, whereby Japan Self-Defence Forces would, for the first time, conduct live-fire training etc., including those involving surface-to-ship missiles, at firing ranges in India,” said a joint statement that also announced that the two sides will deepen security and defence cooperation and hold “bilateral and multilateral exercises at short notice”.
The Ministers also planned a dialogue and tabletop exercise (TTX) involving the consular authorities of India and Japan to help in cases where evacuation of Indian and Japanese nationals would be required.
The two-plus-two dialogue featured Defence Minister Rajnath Singh and External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar and their Japanese counterparts, Toshimitsu Motegi and Shinjiro Koizumi. The Japanese side “explained the ongoing efforts to revise Japan’s National Security Strategy, National Defence Strategy and Defence Buildup Program”. The current government in Japan, led by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, is carrying out several reforms in the country’s strategic and security culture in view of the ongoing wars in West Asia and Ukraine, as well as global trends.
Following the meeting, Mr. Jaishankar said, “Reviewed the entire gamut of our bilateral cooperation, focusing on strengthening economic security and deepening G2G, B2B and P2P linkages. Our discussions also covered challenges and opportunities in the Indo-Pacific, regional hotspots, global issues, and multilateral cooperation.”
The joint statement said the Ministers discussed the UNICORN naval radar system that Japan has proposed for India, and added that an “early formulation” of “Acceptance of Necessity” by February of next year is on track.
Further collaborations
The two sides also discussed enhancing “mine countermeasures capabilities” and “joint development in naval ship building and design”.
“They welcomed the expanding cooperation between the two countries’ coast guards, including the 5th Coast Guard Global Summit (CGGS) to be held in India in February 2027, a framework which was initiated by the Japan Coast Guard,” the statement said.
The Ministers also agreed to deepen information-sharing arrangements between the Japan Maritime Self-Defence Force and the Indian Navy. Welcoming the participation of both countries in the Malabar 2026 multilateral naval exercise and the Japan-India Maritime Exercise (JAIMEX 2026), held in Japan this month, the two sides agreed to expand joint exercises and exchanges between their Special Operations Forces.
Further, they agreed to advance collaboration between the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) and Japan’s Acquisition, Technology and Logistics Agency (ATLA) in advanced missile and defence technologies. They also agreed to promote cooperation in ‘air domain awareness’ and expand multilateral defence engagement in the Indo-Pacific.
In an interview with The Japan News, Mr. Jaishankar said on Thursday (November 19, 2026) that Japan and India, alongside ‘Quad’ partners United States and Australia, would advance a free and open Indo-Pacific through “practical cooperation”. He said, “Japan has a significant role to play in advancing this vision.”

briefs.headline: Removal proceedings against me infructuous after resignation: Justice Varma tells Lok Sabha Secretariat
briefs.deck: In a letter circulated among MPs on November 19, Justice Varma stated that the proceedings directed toward his removal did not survive his resignation
briefs.bodyText:
Justice Yashwant Varma has contended that proceedings for his removal as a High Court judge became infructuous following his resignation and cannot be continued, saying any attempt to remove him from office would be without constitutional foundation.
In a letter dated September 10 to Lok Sabha Secretary General Utpal Kumar Singh, he responded to the report of the inquiry committee constituted by Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla.
Mr. Varma wrote that the proceedings directed towards his removal did not survive his resignation.
He reiterated that he was innocent of the allegations against him, including the suggestion that he possessed ill-gotten funds, and asserted that his resignation should not be construed as an acknowledgement or admission of any allegation or finding.
The letter was circulated among MPs on Thursday (November 19, 2026).
The three-member inquiry committee, in its report tabled in Parliament on August 12, had found all three charges against Justice Varma proved.
The charges related to his failure to explain the presence, source or ownership of cash found at his official residence, failure to secure and preserve material evidence leading to the unexplained disappearance of the currency, and evasive and unsatisfactory explanations during the inquiry.

briefs.headline: IAF’s ‘active Rafale count cut to 32’ by FlightGlobal; Defence Ministry disputes claim
briefs.deck: 36 Rafale fighters were purchased from France; FlightGlobal in late 2025 listed 35 aircraft as active, while the latest edition has reduced the number to 32
briefs.bodyText:
The number of active Rafale fighter jets in the Indian Air Force (IAF) inventory has been revised downward to 32 from 35 in the latest edition of the World Air Forces directory released by British aviation publication FlightGlobal.
However, sources in the Ministry of Defence (MoD) questioned the authenticity of the assessment, saying the information was not provided by the Ministry.
Senior Defence Ministry officials said the figures published in the directory did not originate from the IAF. The latest assessment, compiled using Cirium’s military fleet database, does not specify which aircraft were excluded from the active inventory or the reasons behind the revision.
The Government procured 36 Rafale fighters from France, comprising 28 single-seat EH and eight twin-seat DH variants. FlightGlobal’s 2026 edition, published in late 2025, listed 35 aircraft as active, while the latest edition has reduced the number to 32.
After Operation Sindoor, the IAF said “losses are a part of combat,” but it never disclosed the total number or the types of aircraft involved.
Bridge support for all 36
The official added that, in June this year, the IAF issued a tender seeking “bridge support” for all 36 Rafale aircraft, underlining that the entire fleet remains part of its support and maintenance requirements.
Cirium tracks military aircraft at the individual airframe level using publicly available information, including aircraft sightings, flight-tracking data, and defence-related reporting. Variations in active fleet figures could reflect aircraft undergoing maintenance, upgrades, or structural repairs. However, the latest directory does not provide details to establish the reasons for the reduction.
The publication has also revised the inventory of Pakistan’s Saab 2000 Erieye airborne early warning and control (AEW&C) aircraft from nine to seven.
Meanwhile, India is pursuing the acquisition of 114 additional Rafale fighters from France for the IAF. Separately, the Indian Navy signed a contract in 2025 for 26 Rafale-Marine fighters to operate from its aircraft carriers.
The directory provides an independent assessment of global military aircraft inventories and does not constitute an official disclosure by the Indian Government.

briefs.headline: Kerala High Court says Guruvayur temple staff must treat devotees with respect, maintain calm
briefs.bodyText:
Kerala High Court says Guruvayur temple staff must treat devotees with respect, maintain calm
The court made observations while closing two suo motu proceedings initiated based on complaints by devotees alleging harassment, discrimination, misconduct and threats by temple staff.
Kochi: The Kerala High Court has said employees of Guruvayur temple must treat devotees with respect and maintain the highest standards of civility, while cautioning that crowd management at the temple requires a balance between the interests of devotees and the need to keep queues moving.
A bench of Justices Devan Ramachandran and Basant Balaji made the observations while closing two suo motu proceedings initiated based on complaints by devotees alleging harassment, discrimination, misconduct and threats by temple staff.
"Every devotee visiting the temple is required to be cared for and treated with the utmost degree of decorum and respect," the court said in its judgment dated November 13.
The court said temple employees at every level must act with "the highest degree of equanimity" and should not lose their temper or show anger towards devotees.
At the same time, the bench noted the difficulties of crowd management at a temple like Guruvayur, where devotees seek to spend as much time as possible in front of the deity while hundreds of others wait for darshan.
"It certainly requires, therefore, a fine balance between the rival interests; but whatever be the reason or provocation, an altercation or bad behaviour on the part of any employee cannot be countenanced," it said.
The court was hearing two complaints alleging harassment of devotees, including specific incidents involving the complainants. It noted that the allegations were largely general, though some specific instances were also mentioned.
During the proceedings, the Guruvayur Devaswom Board’s standing counsel told the court that the board would ensure full compliance with its observations.
He also pointed out that there had been instances in the past when devotees provoked staff, including one incident that led to a stabbing.
The court said the responsibility to maintain civility was mutual, warning that poorly handled heated situations could spiral out of control and affect the sanctified atmosphere of the temple.
The court said, since the counsel "undertakes that our observations above will be fully implemented by the Devaswom Board, we deem no further directions necessary in these DBPs (suo motu matter), and they are consequently closed."

briefs.headline: Supreme Court orders counselling for 6-year-old after finding father tutored in violation of order
briefs.bodyText:
Supreme Court.
Credit: PTI Photo
New Delhi: The Supreme Court has directed immediate engagement of a child counsellor for a six-year-old boy retained by his father in alleged violation of a mediated settlement, in an order prioritising the minor’s psychological well-being over immediate enforcement of custody terms in a sensitive dispute.
Experience a more refined e-paper today
A bench of Justices Vikram Nath, Sandeep Mehta and Aparesh Kumar Singh, hearing a contempt petition by the mother, found that the child’s mind “appears to have been severely tutored against the petitioner-mother as well as his sister.”
In its order on November 19, 2026, the court held the father prima facie is in contempt of the court’s December 12, 2025 order that had granted the mother exclusive custody and guardianship, with only limited visitation for the father.
The bench interacted with the child in chambers on November 3 and spoke separately with both parents. It declined to order abrupt restoration of custody, citing the risk of lasting psychological harm.
“Prima facie, the father was in clear contempt,” the bench noted, adding there appeared a conscious attempt to “brainwash and poison the mind of the child against his mother as well as sister.”
From the father’s mannerisms, the court said that he “appears to be displaying clear signs of substance abuse.”
The dispute arose from a transfer petition. During its pendency the parties reached a settlement on November 13, 2025, recorded by the Supreme Court on December 12.
Custody of daughter (then 11) and son (then 6) was to remain with the mother. The father received visitation rights twice a year for four days each at his parental home in Dholpur. He agreed to pay Ra 8,000 monthly for the children’s education and not to claim custody outside the compromise terms.
The mother alleged that on July 22, 2026 the father collected the boy from his school in Mayur Vihar, Delhi, under the pretext of visitation and retained him in Rajasthan. Police complaint and contempt notice yielded no result, prompting the present petition.
The father produced the child on October 12. In his reply he admitted retaining the boy, citing the child’s alleged preference and claims of trauma at the mother’s home.
He said the child was comfortable in Dholpur and attending a local school.
Despite the prima facie finding of contempt, the court held it would be unsafe to force an immediate return. It directed the Dholpur Family Court to engage a counsellor forthwith.
The court ordered the father must present the child for sessions in an influence-free atmosphere within the court premises, with the aim of restoring the child’s trust in his mother and sister. Sessions may begin twice a week.
The father was barred from interference; costs are to be borne by him. The mother may seek limited participation with the counsellor’s approval.
The child may remain in Dholpur until the counsellor’s report reaches the Supreme Court in a sealed cover by January 22, 2027. Both parties and the child must appear in chambers that day. If the counsellor finds the boy ready earlier, the matter may be listed for early orders, the bench said.

briefs.headline: Cyclone Akvan: Landfall process begins near Odisha's Gopalpur
briefs.bodyText:
The national weather agency said in a bulletin, "Latest satellite imagery indicates the land interaction commenced as the sheared cloud mass associated with the cyclonic storm 'Akvan' entered into north Andhra Pradesh-south Odisha coasts."
The wind speed at the commencement of the landfall was 70-90 kmph and the same will continue for the next six hours, it said.
Akvan is the third cyclonic storm in the Bay of Bengal within the last one month. While the other two storms hit the Andhra coast, the newest impact is majorly on Odisha.
The Odisha government has set up 9,299 shelters, evacuated over 1 lakh people to safety, deployed 305 emergency response teams and closed educational institutes in several districts as a precaution.
The state government also deployed 60 teams of Odisha Disaster Rapid Action Force (ODRAF), 14 of National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), and 131 of Fire and Emergency Services, the chief secretary said, adding that more arrangements will be made wherever necessary.
To address possible road blockages, the Odisha Forest Development Corporation has deployed 100 teams.
In Andhra Pradesh, fishermen have been warned not to venture into the sea. With the cyclone moving close to the north Andhra districts, the India Meteorological Department said Srikakulam, Parvathipuram Manyam, Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam, Anakapalle and Kakinada districts would receive extremely heavy rain, while Alluri Sitarama Raju and Konaseema districts would see heavy rain.
People in the coastal areas of north Andhra Pradesh have been asked to remain alert, and farmers to take adequate precautions in farm operations.

Pointing to the absence of medical records, prescriptions or bills, they said no injury had been demonstrated and sought dismissal of the complaint with exemplary costs.
The commission noted that the companies had cited both a seven-day and a 72-hour limit, positions it found contradictory. It observed that the box had been delivered at around 11.45 pm, making it impossible for the complainant to consume all six varieties on the same day. It therefore held that the February 21 complaint was filed within seven days of delivery. It also pointed out that the original wrappers had been produced before it and that the companies had not specifically denied supplying expired chocolates, but had primarily disputed the complaint on the ground of delay.
The commission observed: “It is not the question of replacement of the chocolate box or refund of the amount, as a seller should not keep expired edible things in the shop.” It described the practice of packing good and expired chocolates in the same gift box as “highly condemnable”. It also accepted Prasad's argument that this was done around Christmas and Valentine's Day, when buyers might not check the expiry dates. The commission noted that Blinkit's counsel had not objected to this submission.
Calling it a matter of public health, the commission said many people in cities such as Bengaluru depended on online platforms and that taking advantage of their trust was unfair.
Holding that the companies had supplied expired chocolates despite knowing that they had expired two months before delivery, the commission found them guilty of deficiency in service and unfair trade practice. The bench, comprising president Vijaykumar M Pawale, member Chandrashekar S Noola and lady member K Anita Shivakumar, partly allowed the complaint on November 6.
In the order authored by K Anita Shivakumar, the commission directed both companies to jointly refund Rs 479 and pay Rs 3,000 as compensation for mental agony and hardship. It also imposed punitive damages of Rs 40,000 under Section 39(1)(g) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, to be remitted to the Consumer Welfare Fund.

stories.headline: Can HMT wind back to the good ol’ times?
stories.deck: Strapping on an HMT watch is a badge of pride. Now, millennials and Gen Z are also jumping on the bandwagon, driving a fresh wave of enthusiasm. What exactly is making this Bengaluru-born legacy brand to tick again? Chetan B.C. explores...
stories.bodyText:
Nothing was going right for Monika, a techie in Mysuru, on November 2. Her boss was giving her an hour-long lecture about work, but a phone call at that moment changed her mood. The phone displayed “watch” on the screen, and Monika was no longer thinking about work. The call meant she had managed to get two limited-edition HMT watches.
“My fiancé’s birthday was on November 10 and our engagement on November 13. I wanted to gift both of us HMT Gandabherunda watches to mark the occasion. The watch holds something we share — pride in our language and land,” she said.
Monika had visited the HMT store at Jalahalli in Bengaluru at least four times but had failed to get a watch. On October 27, she requested the staff at HMT to help her secure a watch and one had a bright idea. Following his suggestion, she enlisted the help of a shopkeeper who had his shop close to the HMT store. When the stock came in, the shopkeeper could quickly dash across and get her two watches. His number was saved as “watch” on her phone.
The golden era
For R. Balu, who works at the HMT shop in Barton Centre on M.G. Road and who previously worked at the Tumakuru division from 1987, this story brings a rush of nostalgia. It reminded him of the “golden era of HMT watches” in the 1970s and 1980s.
“Indian weddings, across north and south India, had one thing in common -- the bride’s family gifting an HMT watch, especially from the Kanchan series, to the groom. People used to refer to Kanchan watches as the wedding watch,” Balu recalled. “I still have mine at home.” He now wears an HMT Avinash.
HMT watches, as Balu noted, have long been synonymous with weddings, friendships, and love stories. Now, a similar interest has resurfaced, although even HMT is trying to figure out the exact reason. On August 15, crowds queued for nearly two kilometres to buy the Gandabherunda watch. On November 1, the HMT Kannadiga watch was unveiled, and about 3,000 watches were sold the next day.
An internal demand survey by HMT pegged the demand for watches at one lakh a month, a figure the company would not have dreamt of achieving three years ago. However, its current installed capacity to assemble watches stands at just 10,000 a month, demand outstripping supply by 10 times.
There is a buzz around the brand once again. But can this “trend” be sustained to give the trademark Public Sector Undertaking Hindustan Machine Tools (HMT) a new lease of life in the long run?
HMT was among the earliest PSUs to mark the emergence of an industrial India, a Nehruvian dream. It supported other PSUs and strategic sectors, by designing, developing, manufacturing and supplying import-substitute industrial mother machines. It employed thousands and also played a significant role in training some of the country’s earliest engineers.
While post-liberalisation meant a complete change of ethos and economics, N. Ramesh Kumar, chairman and MD of HMT, told The Hindu that revival efforts were under way across HMT, which has three verticals, including watches. On the watch front, the company is in the process of scaling up production by next year.
Two-year production gap
In 2016, HMT called time on the operations of its watch division, although the sale of watches continued. However, Ramesh Kumar said there was no production between 2016 and 2018. The credit belonged to longtime employees of HMT’s production division, who wanted to continue their work before the entire operation was shut down.
“From 2019, with whatever inventory remained, new watches were made and sold,” he said. It was in 2025, that the brand caught a fresh wave of momentum.
The impetus for mass production came on August 15, 2026, when buyers formed the long queue, all for a chance to own the Gandabherunda watch. The queue included a woman with her newborn.
Ramesh Kumar displayed a newspaper clipping from 1976 featuring a long queue of people waiting to buy watches, drawing a parallel with a similar incident near HMT Bhavan on October 26, 2026. Long queues like these have now become a familiar sight.
Balu teared up as he spoke about the long queues to buy watches over the last few months. “We call for police backup for crowd control during restocking. I wish the earlier glory days return. Many families will be fed if that happens.”
What sparked the buzz?
Over the last month, The Hindu visited all four HMT stores — Jalahalli, the Souvenir Shop, HMT Bhavan, and Barton Centre — on multiple occasions and found people enquiring about watches, particularly the Gandabherunda. The Barton Centre store now has a register containing the names and phone numbers of over 1,000 people who have “pre-booked” watches. The list also features senior IPS and IAS officers.
When this reporter asked over 50 people what drew them to the HMT brand, one common factor emerged: social media posts evoking regional identity or a personal connection to the brand. For instance, Ravi Kumar, a native of Tumakuru who visited HMT Bhavan, said social media helped him learn about HMT’s legacy.
“HMT is deeply connected to the Indian history of industrialisation, besides carrying regional essence through its design and Kannada numerals on the dial,” Ravi Kumar said, stressing its association with identity. “Series like Janata and Pilot, and the watches crafted for ISRO, the Army, and the Air Force — all of these make me proud to wear the brand,” he added.
Several respondents said the brand had become a topic of conversation in office spaces. Umang Nagda, who works at a cybersecurity firm in Mumbai, his hometown, said his boss, who is from Kerala, had spoken about HMT on several occasions. “I didn’t know there was such a brand with a deep-rooted national legacy,” Umang said. He was at an HMT store with a friend to buy a watch as a birthday gift for his boss.
Many said they had been tracking HMT watch stocks through social media and were eager to buy a watch from a brand their parents or grandparents once owned. One particular response stood out: vintage watches were seen as accessories that pair well with formal attire. Many officegoers said HMT watches attracted attention.
Yadu Krishna, deputy manager of HMT’s production wing, said fast-moving watches included the Gandabherunda, Kohinoor, Tariq, Stellar, Sona, Himalaya, and Vijay. “These watches are currently being mass-produced,” he said.
HMT shopkeepers said the watches went out of stock within a day or two of restocking, underscoring the interest among the younger generation. Many described the designs as “elegant”.
Market observation
Bharath Kumar, a collector who posts updates about watches on Instagram under the handle ‘ticking_time_’ said that the current wave could well be driven by nostalgia, amplified by social media. He said it has given the brand a good opportunity for revival if it makes the right moves.
Bharath Kumar said HMT currently outsources component manufacturing, including watch cases, and only assembles the watches locally. He stressed that bringing all operations back in-house would lend the watches a true sense of being regionally manufactured. “There is also the need to strengthen the research and development wing to keep pace with current trends. Riding only on the current traction will not sustain the momentum,” he said.
He also noted that if there is reluctance to invest in R&D and production, the revival efforts would amount to very little in the long run.
Is there a market?
Shaik Mehmood of Vintage Times on Commercial Street explained that HMT needs to move towards mechanical watches to retain demand.
“HMT still carries great brand equity. What it needs now is an upgrade keeping in mind the future and long-term needs of users. Quartz watches are doing well for the brand now because of its brand equity, but mechanical watches will drive the demand,” he said, adding that the PSU needs to increase its production capacity quickly.
He said that Gen Z and millennial consumers are currently looking for ways to stand out through distinctive brands and designs. They are always on the look out for watches made from scratch and are rare in the market. International watchmakers producing mechanical watches have priced them higher because of the growing demand for such timepieces.
“HMT already has designs for such watches, and vintage designs themselves are a USP now. So, the brand should produce mechanical watches at lower costs, which is exactly the essence of HMT,” he said.
Bharath Kumar added that watch collectors are increasingly focusing on these pieces. He further explained that while luxury watches are thriving internationally and micro-brands, including watch companies named after cities, are doing well, mid-range brands are struggling.
Research and cuurent situation
Gubbi Prakash, former HMT executive, said production and research were among the PSU’s strongest areas during its heydays.
For instance, until recently, HMT remained the only major brand on record to have developed watch movements in-house, although another brand recently claimed to have achieved the same. In the olden days, HMT designed dials, manufactured cases, and assembled watches at its own factories. Experts maintained that this is precisely what HMT needs to go back to, if it wants to capitalise on the current momentum.
HMT began operations in 1953 and set up its watch division in 1961. The first watch, Janata, was launched in collaboration with Japanese firm Citizen. A former chairman and Managing Director of HMT said Citizen also witnessed significant growth through its collaboration with HMT. By the 1990s, HMT was manufacturing every watch component, barring quartz, in-house. HMT were also the first to bring quartz watches to India.
In the field of precision technology, HMT conducted research and improved watch movements, helping it produce some of the country’s well-known watches.
Gubbi Prakash said the movement developed by Citizen initially had nearly 127 components. Research and development efforts subsequently brought the number down to 106-107, with the results bearing fruit in the form of the HMT Sona edition. “It was the slimmest watch we produced at that time and it became a huge hit,” he said.
At least two former Managing Directors said HMT’s decline began with the emergence of an Indian competitor. The situation worsened after the liberalisation of 1991, which brought more brands to India, along with quartz watches. As the PSU came under increasing pressure, several agents began producing counterfeits. Cash flow declined and the PSU was unable to keep pace with the rapidly growing market.
M.S. Zahed, former chairman and Managing Director of HMT, said the PSU needed to expand its assembly units. “Earlier, there were several assembly units in different districts. This should be brought back. Units can be established in other districts of Karnataka, and the State market should be captured first,” he said.
What is being done now
Ramesh Kumar, the current chairman of HMT, explained that the primary focus has been on gathering field-level intelligence through direct interactions with customers. “Designs are being approached through the customers’ lens, and even complaints about the watch straps are being examined and researched to make them better,” he said. He also noted that three new designs were in the making. Simultaneously, the installed production capacity was being expanded.
Amid increasing demand from the public, HMT is undertaking order-based production as it did when it mass-produced watches for the Bangalore Development Authority’s 50th anniversary last year.
On whether mechanical watches would be introduced, Ramesh Kumar said the proposal was currently under discussion. He said production was progressing well and that the ultimate goal was to bring back the brand’s glorious days of end-to-end manufacturing in-house.
Threat of counterfeiting
According to sources in the HMT, counterfeiting has also been a major concern. Over the last five months, more than 12 legal notices were issued to unauthorised sellers in the market.
HMT operates four of its own centres and an online store. Amazon also serves as an online sales platform for the brand. No other seller is authorised to sell new HMT watches. “Duplication is visible, but the market is thriving,” said Ramesh Kumar on the counterfeit market.
While challenges persist, sources said revival efforts were now being pursued in a focused and well-planned manner. If things go as per plan, enthusiasts may not have to devise elaborate schemes to get their hands on a watch from this legacy brand.

stories.headline: BJP will firmly oppose any bid to scrap Karnataka’s anti-conversion, anti-cow slaughter laws in winter session, says opposition leader R Ashoka
stories.deck: Opposition party also plans to raise drought, price rise, sting operation and administrative failure during winter sessio
stories.bodyText:
Mangaluru:
BJP
 will strongly oppose any Congress govt move to repeal the anti-conversion and anti-cow slaughter laws during the Karnataka Legislature’s winter session, leader of opposition R Ashoka said Tuesday.
“If the govt moves to repeal the laws, we will firmly resist it,” Ashoka told reporters. The BJP would also corner the govt over 
drought
, price rise, sting operation and administrative failure, he said.
Ashoka said higher milk prices and KSRTC bus fares had burdened people. The govt could have averted the fare hike by releasing Rs 5,000 crore owed to the corporation on time, he said.
He said the govt would have to borrow around Rs 1.5 lakh crore in the March budget. He also criticised chief minister 
DK Shivakumar
 over alleged spending on his official residence, ‘Ganga Krupa’.
Citing the Rs 32,000 crore announcement at the Mangaluru cabinet meeting, Ashoka challenged the chief minister to release at least Rs 3,000 crore to Mangaluru City Corporation.
He accused the govt of burdening people to fund its five guarantee schemes. The BJP was not against the schemes, but they should not be funded through additional taxes, he said.
He said the “bankrupt govt” had failed to provide schoolchildren with mid-day meals. 
Villagers in Haveri pooled money for meals at their local government school after funds went unreleased for nearly a month, he said.
‘Vote bank politics’
Ashoka criticised the govt’s decision to transfer money to minority students’ accounts for laptops and provide them with armed forces training.
He said the Congress govt had invited tenders for a 60-day army training programme exclusively for minorities. Armed forces recruitment was not religion-based, but Congress wanted to appease minorities for votes, he said.
He said the govt was giving only minority students Rs 50,000 through DBT for laptops, sidelining other communities. Allocations for minorities were rising each year while those for other communities fell, he said, calling it Congress’s ‘vote bank politics’.

stories.headline: SIR: Deleted EPIC numbers ‘reissued’ to different names in Bengaluru
stories.deck: In hundreds of cases across Bengaluru, EPIC numbers of people marked for deletion during the SIR have been reissued to other individuals, violating the ECI manual’s requirement that every elector have a unique EPIC number
stories.bodyText:
In at least 290 cases across Bengaluru, The Hindu found that Electors Photo Identity Card (EPIC) numbers belonging to people marked for deletion for being marked “Absent, Shifted, Dead or Duplicate” during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) have been transferred or reissued to different individuals in the final electoral roll, indicating that an EPIC number that identified one person before the SIR is now being used to identify someone else.
The Election Commission of India’s (ECI) Handbook for Electoral Registration Officers explicitly prohibits the reuse of an EPIC number once it has been issued to a person. It states that the software used to generate EPIC numbers must keep track of numbers already issued and ensure that “the EPIC number once utilized, are not used again.” In other words, an EPIC number issued to one person cannot be reassigned to another person. It also states that “all efforts have to be made to ensure ‘universality, uniqueness and permanence of EPIC’ details of an elector.”
To identify these cases, The Hindu compared the ASDD list with the final SIR roll, matching EPIC numbers against the names of people listed for deletion and those appearing in the final roll. The comparison found that the same EPIC numbers that were marked for deletion are now appearing against different individuals.
Many such cases were found to be concentrated in Bengaluru’s Dasarahalli Assembly constituency.
For instance, Shashikumar, who was enrolled in Dasarahalli (Part No. 103), was marked as “dead” and deleted. His EPIC number has now been reissued to Chandramma in Part No. 273 of the same constituency. Similarly, Roopa, who was enrolled in Dasarahalli (Part No. 107), was marked as “absent” and deleted. Her EPIC number has been reissued to Pallavi in Part No. 174 of the same constituency.
In another case, Kariyappa, 41, who was enrolled in Dasarahalli (Part No. 109), was marked as “absent” and deleted. His EPIC number now appears against Vijayashree’s name in Part No. 53 of the same constituency. Similarly, Shivanna, who was enrolled in Part No. 109 in Dasarahalli and marked for deletion as he had “shifted”, now has his EPIC number listed against Tejashwini’s name in Part No. 57.
The Hindu shared sample EPIC numbers with the Chief Electoral Officer’s (CEO) office, seeking an explanation for the discrepancies. CEO V. Anbu Kumar said he would examine the cases and could not comment before that.

briefs.headline: ‘AI can’t replace the human side of rock’
briefs.deck: Bengaluru-based rock band Steel Falcon’s guitarist Nathanael Barna talks about drawing inspiration from classic rock, the growing influence of AI on music and more
briefs.bodyText:
Classic rock may be rooted in different times and eras, but Bengaluru-based rock band Steel Falcon is all set to give it a fresh voice. Drawing inspiration from bands such as Led Zeppelin, Guns N’ Roses and Whitesnake, the band is bringing Monsters of Rock, a tribute to classic hard rock, to Cahoots on November 21, before heading to Nagaland for the Hornbill Festival.
‘Keeping the sound of classic rock alive’
The band is also working on their album, drawing inspiration from the rock music of the 1950s-90s era. The album, which is currently in the mastering stage, is yet to be titled. Guitarist Nathanael Barna says the band hopes to bring the sound and spirit of that era to a contemporary audience. “The quality of musicianship and songwriting from that era is something special. Songs came from personal experiences, whether it was love, breakups or political issues, which made them relatable. We want to bring back some of that sound, but with a modern twist. It's not just a clone or a rip-off of that time. It's something new,” he says.
‘AI hasn’t lived a human life or experienced anything close to humanity’
Nathanael believes music is deeply connected to human emotions and experiences, something he feels AI cannot replicate. “Music is all about the human experience. If you look at every musician or artiste who is out there today, what do they write about? They write about their personal experiences. 
AI hasn't lived a human life; it hasn't had a human experience. So how could it possibly know about music or what exactly we're talking about, how we feel?” he says.
‘Independent musicians need a fair chance’
When it comes to streaming platforms, he believes algorithms can help listeners discover music, but their preference for commercial sounds often leaves independent musicians struggling for visibility. “Independent musicians don't get discovered because the algorithm suggests only a certain kind of music. And the algorithm favours commercial music. It is something that needs to be addressed. Streaming platforms should have separate categories for independent musicians and AI-generated music, along with stricter guidelines on the use of AI,” Nathanael emphasised.
Today anybody can sit in their bedroom, open up their laptop, download a couple of software programmes, give some prompts and then have a song ready. But nobody did anything. It was all made by a computer. I feel like it is unfair to us as artistes who work hard and strive to hone our craft every single day. AI has got its uses, but music isn't one of them
Nathanael Barna

briefs.headline: The 45-minute act: Three plays explore the world of Girish Karnad this weekend in Bengaluru
briefs.bodyText:
What if a play that usually runs for nearly two hours could be experienced in just 45 minutes? Organizational Theatre is bringing this format to the stage with a festival featuring three plays by playwright 
Girish Karnad
, each adapted into a 45-minute production at Alliance Francaise on November 22. Directed by Sanjay Singh, Punkaj Gupta and Jharna Gupta, the productions are part of the theatre group's director-mentoring programme, which allows experienced actors to train as directors and take a production from concept to stage. The festival will offer audiences a chance to experience different themes and interpretations of Karnad's work in a single programme.
Making room for three plays
The idea of presenting each play in 45 minutes came from Ranji David, founder of Organizational Theatre, to attempt to make the festival a varied yet engaging experience for audiences. “The initial idea was to do 30 minutes, but when the directors began working on the plays, they felt that it was too little. We then settled on 45 minutes, which would do justice to the productions,” he shares. The original stories remain unchanged, with the directors focusing on retaining their essence while adapting them to the shorter duration. “This allows audiences to see different kinds of work by Karnad and appreciate how different directors approach his writing,” adds Ranji. Each production will be followed by a five-minute interval, during which a narrator will introduce the next play and its cast while the stage is reset.
Theatre practitioners must give space to newcomers and groom them as directors; we are creating an ecosystem of people who can carry forward the philosophy and legacy of theatre in Bengaluru

briefs.headline: Bengaluru restaurant fined Rs 10,000 for charging Rs 15 for branded food takeaway bag
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 A Rs 15 takeaway bag has proved costly for Meghana Foods restaurant. The Bengaluru Urban 4th additional district consumer disputes redressal commission recently held the restaurant guilty of unfair trade practice and deficiency in service for charging a Girinagar resident Rs 15 for a carry bag bearing its name and logo. The restaurant has been ordered to pay Rs 10,000 in damages.
On May 8, 2026, Pranava KN, 25, ordered a paneer biryani from Meghana Foods on Dr Rajkumar Road, Rajajinagar, through 
Zomato
. The restaurant’s invoice listed the food and, separately, a “restaurant packaging charge” of Rs 15. With GST added, that became Rs 15.7, and the restaurant invoice came to Rs 451.5. Pranava also said a separate platform fee of Rs 17.5 was charged. The carry bag and other packaging carried the restaurant’s name, logo and brand identity.
Pranava said the packaging was not plain or neutral but worked as a medium of advertisement and brand promotion. It travelled outside the restaurant and exposed its name to third persons, while he paid for it. In his view, the restaurant got a dual advantage: money from the customer for packaging and free publicity from the same packaging, which amounted to unjust enrichment. 
A consumer, he argued, cannot be made to fund the advertising for the very place he buys from. He added that this was not an isolated instance and that he had earlier issued similar legal notices to Zomato and other restaurants.
He raised the issue with Zomato and the restaurant by email and sent a legal notice on Aug 5. Nobody replied. On Aug 27, he approached the consumer commission.
Despite receiving notice from the commission, Meghana Foods neither appeared nor filed its version of events, and was placed ex parte. The notice to Zomato came back unserved, and Pranava filed a memo saying he did not wish to pursue the case against it; thus, the complaint against Zomato was dismissed as not pressed. The commission, comprising president Vijaykumar M Pawale and members Chandrashekar S Noola and K Anita Shivakumar, said that if the restaurant were genuine in its attitude, it could simply have supplied packaging without its name and logo. It added that the practice “should not continue hereafter.”
It noted that Meghana Foods’ failure to appear before the forum amounted to an admission of the allegations, leaving the complainant’s evidence unchallenged, and that the restaurant had also failed to redress his grievance when it was first raised.
On Nov 12, the commission directed the restaurant to pay Rs 5,000 in global compensation, covering the Rs 15 refund, compensation and litigation costs, and another Rs 5,000 in punitive damages, to be deposited in the commission’s consumer legal aid account. Both sums are due within 45 days from the date of order, failing which interest at 8% will apply.

briefs.headline: Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026: Startup’s AI device targets traffic violations
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: Bengaluru-based startup Radiantech Systems has developed a ruggedised AI edge-computing device designed to reduce the bandwidth, storage and server demands of AI-powered traffic surveillance. The hardware, named RTE-300-R Rugged High Performance Edge AI Compute, was showcased at the Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026.
The device processes traffic camera footage locally at road junctions instead of continuously transmitting massive volumes of raw video to centralised servers. Once a violation, such as jumping a red light, is detected, only a brief alert detailing the incident is sent to the city command centre.
Explaining the need for the technology, Radiantech Systems CEO Sumanth S said a network of 10,000 cameras, each transmitting 3–4 MB of data per second, could generate around 40,000 Mbps of continuous backhaul traffic. Such volumes increase bandwidth, storage and computing requirements, pushing authorities towards expensive GPU-powered data centres.
The RTE-300-R aims to address this challenge through local processing. 
Designed for harsh outdoor conditions, the ruggedised, air-cooled unit eliminates the need for expensive, water-intensive cooling infrastructure. It can also store footage locally for 60 days, allowing authorities to retrieve specific clips when required, before automatically deleting the files.
Radiantech has submitted a formal proposal to the Bengaluru Traffic Police (BTP), which has expressed interest in the architecture. The company is awaiting a Letter of Intent (LoI).
Positioning itself as a hardware systems manufacturer, Radiantech plans to collaborate with third-party software developers to deploy AI-based violation-detection models on its devices. The approach could help cities reduce infrastructure costs while making AI-driven traffic enforcement more efficient and scalable.

briefs.headline: Karnataka High Court grants relief to medical seat aspirant, says mere possession of mobile phone cannot be termed ‘unfair means’
briefs.deck: The court said a breach of discipline and the procurement of merit by deception are not necessarily synonymous, rejecting NTA’s contentions that carrying a prohibited electronic device into examination premises itself constituted an unfair means practice, irrespective of whether it was actually used
briefs.bodyText:
The Karnataka High Court has quashed the National Testing Agency’s (NTA) decision to withhold the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination result of a medical student over an allegation that she had carried a mobile phone into an earlier examination that was subsequently cancelled.
A Division Bench comprising Justice M. Nagaprasanna and Justice Hema Kulkarni allowed a petition filed by a 20-year-old girl from Ranebennur in Haveri district and directed the NTA to issue her scorecard without any remark indicating that her result was withheld or cancelled.
Seat confirmed
The bench also confirmed a medical seat allotted to her in a government medical college in Karnataka based on her rank secured in the re-NEET held on June 21, following the interim order passed by the court earlier allowing her to participate in the seat selection process.
The student had appeared for the NEET examination conducted on May 3. However, the NTA cancelled the examination following widespread allegations of question paper leakage and other malpractices and announced a fresh examination on June 21.
After issuing a fresh admit card to the student for the re-NEET, the NTA served her a show-cause notice on June 17, alleging that she had carried a mobile phone into the examination premises during the May 3 examination. Her result of the re-NEET was withheld even though she had scored 570 marks out of the total 720 marks.
Carried inadvertently
The student, in her reply to the show-cause notice, contended that she carried the mobile phone in her pocket inadvertently due to examination anxiety and stress and had never used it. The examination centre authorities had found no incriminating activity on the mobile phone after detecting it, it was contended.
However, the NTA defended its action, arguing that carrying a prohibited electronic device into examination premises itself constituted an unfair means practice, irrespective of whether it was actually used.
“It must be remembered that the mere possession of a mobile phone, though capable of constituting a breach of examination instructions, cannot, without regard to the governing rules and attendant circumstances, invariably be equated with the actual use of unfair means to secure an undeserved academic advantage. A breach of discipline and the procurement of merit by deception are not necessarily synonymous,” the bench said while rejecting the NTA’s contentions.
Noting that the student appeared in the re-NEET without any allegation of violation of norm and had secured a rank that earned her a merit seat, the bench said that “the law must be firm against dishonesty, but it need not be unforgiving towards every inadvertent lapse. An examination authority must be vigilant against malpractice, but vigilance cannot degenerate into rigidity that defeats the very purpose of the examination.”

briefs.headline: First runner-up at Ticket to Hornbill, rock band Steel Falcon will perform in Bengaluru on November 21
briefs.deck: The Bengaluru-based band is gearing up for a showdown at the prestigious Hornbill Festival in Nagaland and the release of their debut album
briefs.bodyText:
The journey of Bengaluru-based rock band Steel Falcon began when three brothers, guitarist Nathanael Barna, bassist Jonathan Barna and percussionist Joshua Barna, working as session musicians, decided to carve out their own space in the rock and metal circuit. They formed the band in 2017 with two other artistes. While those two left later, two others joined, vocalist Alan Thomas and keyboardist Sunil Manohar, in 2023 and 2024, thus completing the ensemble.
Set to play in Bengaluru, on November 21, the band is on a hot streak after being crowned first runner-up at Ticket to Hornbill 2026, held in Delhi, earlier this month. It is a nationwide competition where bands compete to perform at the prestigious Hornbill Festival in Nagaland.
Nathanael says, “Hornbill was actually something that we grew up fantasising about. It promises national recognition that would help us pursue music as a career. It’s a very hard contest to crack with bands from all over the country participating. It’s a challenge even to get shortlisted.”
This year, 222 bands participated in the event, with 12 shortlisted for the prelims in Delhi, and five bands participating in the final. The top three bands will perform at the festival to be held in Kohima, from December 1 to 10. Terat, a band from Mizoram, won first place, while Nchanter from Uttarakhand secured third place.
“We had the time of our lives playing to an audience that loves and adores the genre we play. The judging panel had members of Parikrama, who are pioneers of the rock music scene in India, and they saw potential in us as well,” says Nathanael.
Debut album
Steel Falcon is also gearing up to release its first album, with some songs being written by Nathanael as early as 2011, when he was in college. The album, which has been in the pipeline since 2023, is set for release in January 2027. “Hornbill is actually a way for us to recover the money that we spent on making the album,” jokes Nathanael. “We didn’t want to hand it over to a label and lose the ownership of our music.”
The untitled album features 13 songs. Nathanael says, “It is a combination of up-tempo, fast-paced numbers with softer love songs, inspired by the music we grew up listening to. The listeners can expect to hear influences from the ‘70s, ‘80s and ‘90s, but with a modern twist, striking a balance between the classic era and the modern era of rock and metal.”
The band dabbles in the sub-genres of rock and metal such as blues rock, heavy rock and glam rock, among others, in the album, with influences from bands such as Kiss, Guns N’ Roses, The Scorpions, The Eagles, White Snake, Def Leppard, Led Zeppelin, The Beatles and Bee Gees. “Our personal influences are also diverse. For example, for my keyboard player Sunil, one of his biggest influences is Ilaiyaraaja, but he also loves Pink Floyd. So, there’s a huge spectrum between these two artistes. My vocalist Alan loves everybody from Frank Sinatra to Avenged Sevenfold,” says Nathanael.
He adds, “The influence of rock music in our lives is something that drove us to form a band that would end up writing its own rock tunes. For some of us, our parents played a huge role in developing a taste for this genre.”
Asked about reviving old songs to create a new album, Nathanael says, “As artistes, we keep getting inspired every day. Inspiration can come from anywhere, and our influences do change and as we grow as musicians. But we have immense love and adoration for the kind of style in which we have written our songs. It is influenced and inspired by those eras, which is at the core of everything we do, regardless of how our tastes might change tomorrow. Everything else is a bonus which gives us room to experiment with different flavours and sounds.”

briefs.headline: Meet Bengaluru’s classically trained duo who enjoy headbanging
briefs.deck: On their debut album Kurukshetra, Bengaluru music duo Aditya and Prerna show us how flexible Indian classical music is – making its way into the realms of metal, rock, jazz and more
briefs.bodyText:
Flautist Aditya Rajaram and violinist Prerna V have already made plenty of waves online, offering powerful and intriguing snippets of their songs and of course, after appearing on Season Two of YouTube-streamed talent show India’s Got Latent, hosted by comedian Samay Raina.
Far from that kind of (arguably) fleeting spotlight that the Internet gives, Aditya and Prerna’s album is an eight-track that swerves between the cinematic title track ‘Kurukshetra’ but before that, opens with the calm-before-the-storm whirlwind song ‘Metal Mohana.’
While it might seem like wide-ranging experiments from the unbound minds of two young artistes, Prerna notes that their album Kurukshetra is bound together by the idea that they are two protagonists who “are a manifestation of the universe experiencing itself.”
She explains, “The album captures intricacies that celebrate the moments they share, ranging from comfort and solace to cognitive dissonance and responsibilities they must conquer.” The violinist says Kurukshetra represents the last hurdle these protagonists face together and treat it less as an “ultimate destination”.
Having seen Aditya and Prerna at the 24 Songs Festival in April this year — just a month after they came together in March — the duo seemed resolute in their genre-bending approach from the start, as evidenced by their performance of ‘Metal Mohana’.
Their classical chops were standout, and Aditya notes that they don’t see a distinction between Indian classical music and metal. “Music just flows through us on autopilot when we’re composing,” he says.
After about seven months of viral fame, several more shows, and now their debut album prepped, Aditya and Prerna perform at The Humming Tree in Indiranagar on November 19 to launch the Kurukshetra album. The duo’s live band setup includes guitarist Advait Pattanaik, bassist Harsh Makam, drummer Saathvik Raghavendra and keyboardist Remmy Martin.
Prerna says, “In addition to this, we will be joined by guest artistes Shamith Kalkur on the mridangam, bringing a taste of South Indian percussive techniques, juxtaposed with Siri Hebbale bringing it in with ferocious metal growls.” The launch show also brings in indie artiste Chinmayi L, debuting her Kannada songs, and Malayalam singer-producer Ahin Viswam. “All in all, we can promise a scrumptious blend of flavours coming together,” Aditya says.
Work on a second album has already been underway (with a few teasers put out on their social media pages), but the duo are keen to focus on Kurukshetra for the concert, considering it is the album launch. There will be a bit of local music represented as well.
Aditya says, “For this show, we’ve curated compositions that Karnataka would have heard while growing up. Renditions that are intimate, interpreted with rock energy.”
If Kurukshetra comes across as a culmination of ideas between the duo, Prerna looks back at the creative process as hugely nourishing. Much like Aditya talking about composing music together as though on autopilot, Prerna says, “We tend to bring out the best in each other. On and off work I have found a safe refuge in Aditya where I can go crazy without applying the conventional ‘rationale’, and he always knows how to complement it best.”
The duo don’t shy away from being seen as a couple, which became one of the talking points of their India’s Got Latent appearance. If it seemed like the reality show format and the host’s playful questions were trying to take the focus away from the music, Aditya and Prerna say they are grateful that “people could eventually connect not only with our music, but also with us as two souls that come together as one force to be reckoned with”.
This is heard in their songs as well, especially the final two songs on the album. There’s a nostalgia-tinged simplicity and warmth in ‘Monsoon Polaroid,’ which was written right after their Latent episode was shot. It draws from the artistes’ childhood and how Carnatic music was a shared constant.
“I grew up in the UK, starting off with Western classical and learning Carnatic after we came back. Aditya learnt Carnatic as a child and got into the indie rock scene shortly after. “Carnatic music has become a medium that we could borrow from to express what words couldn’t,” Prerna says.
Aditya sets a different scene for the song and says, “‘Monsoon Polaroid’ celebrates a parallel between the comfort of smelling the first drop of water on the dry ground and the aroma of menshinkayi or mirchi bajjis with filter coffee from your parents’ kitchen.”
The galloping final track ‘Sharbét’ is a resounding sign-off from the duo, channelling rollercoaster emotions through rock, fusion and jazz, prog metal (in that order) packed together in under four minutes. “It was born out of an exaggerated scenario in our heads where we get caught by our parents and were running away, but realise that we get to do this together,” Prerna says.
Between the two of them, Prerna is most excited to see how ‘Sharbét’ will be received. “Composing ‘Sharbét’ was like a game of ping-pong for the two of us. Aditya wrote parts that were completely bizarre, and I would take them in a completely different direction to gel together, and send it back,” she says.
Aditya is keen to see how ‘Monsoon Polaroid’ will do. “I wanted this to be a song that the audience can sing along to, and find comfort in. A song that feels like a hug from your mother,” he says.
A second album is already in the works. Prerna says there are a lot more metal, synths, and trippy soundscapes. “And a statement that we never intend to stop. The next chapter of Aditya and Prerna places the protagonists in the middle of a distant future, where the highs and lows of being born as a human exist, but are imagined in far different contexts,” she explains.
In the meantime, the duo are planning to take Kurukshetra places, kickstarting a tour in November and December through the artiste and event company Quriosity. “We will perform at the Abhivyakti Festival in Ahmedabad, among other shows soon to be announced,” Prerna adds.

stories.headline: Anthropic raises $81 billion in IPO amid AI market volatility
stories.deck: The Claude maker priced its shares at $83 apiece, implying an equity valuation of about $1.03 trillion based on outstanding shares, with trading scheduled to begin on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on November 19
stories.bodyText:
Anthropic, the maker of artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude, has priced its initial public offering (IPO) at $83 a share, valuing the offering at approximately $81.34 billion, according to an announcement by the company on November 18.
The company said its shares were expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on November 19 under the ticker symbol ANT. The offering is expected to close on November 20, subject to customary closing conditions.
According to Anthropic’s announcement, the offering comprises 980 million shares of Class A common stock. Of these, 956.35 million shares are being sold by the company and 23.65 million by existing shareholders. Anthropic said it would not receive any proceeds from the sale of shares by the selling shareholders.
At the IPO price of $83 a share, the company’s portion of the offering is valued at approximately $79.38 billion, while the shares sold by existing shareholders are valued at approximately $1.96 billion. These figures are before underwriting discounts and expenses.
At $83 a share, Anthropic’s overall equity value works out to approximately $1.03 trillion, based on the total number of shares outstanding after the IPO.
Anthropic has also given the banks (underwriters) managing the IPO the option to purchase an additional 147 million shares within 30 days, potentially increasing the size of the offering.
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the lead underwriters for the IPO, with JPMorgan, Citigroup, Barclays and other investment banks also participating, according to the SEC filing.
The IPO comes amid growing investor concerns over the sustainability of the AI investment boom and whether technology companies can generate sufficient returns from their infrastructure spending.
On November 5, the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5%, wiping out trillions of dollars in market value, while NVIDIA shares declined 9% and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped 12%.
Earlier, on October 29, Alphabet shares plunged 12.6%, wiping out approximately $500 billion in market value after its quarterly results raised concerns over its advertising business and the cash-flow impact of rising AI investments. The sell-off reflected broader concerns over the valuations of AI-linked companies and the returns from their heavy spending on data centres and computing infrastructure.
The broader U.S. market opened higher on Thursday, with the Nasdaq Composite gaining 1.55% at the opening bell at 9.30 am U.S. Eastern Time (8 pm IST), according to Reuters.
Anthropic’s shares had yet to begin trading as of 10.45 am US ET (9.15 pm IST), with The Wall Street Journal reporting that early indications pointed to an opening price of around $104, about 25% above the IPO price of $83. Reuters had earlier reported an indicative price of $99.82 at 9.50 a.m. U.S. ET (8.20 p.m. IST).

stories.headline: SEBI, PFRDA call for deeper capital markets to fund Viksit Bharat 2047
stories.deck: Sustained participation by retail investors and domestic institutional investors (DIIs) had helped Indian markets remain resilient amid volatility caused by foreign portfolio investor outflows over the past year.
stories.bodyText:
India will need deeper capital markets and greater mobilisation of long-term domestic savings to finance its Viksit Bharat 2047 ambition, as traditional bank lending and government expenditure alone may not be sufficient to meet the country’s growing funding requirements, Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) Whole-Time Member K.V.R. Murty said.
“Sustaining a real GDP growth trajectory of around 8.0% would require greater mobilisation of domestic household savings and global institutional funds through transparent securities markets,” Mr. Murty said at the CII Financing Summit 2026 in Mumbai.
He underscored the need to deepen debt and equity markets to complement bank financing and public capital expenditure, particularly for infrastructure and long-gestation projects. Strengthening market infrastructure, cybersecurity and investor protection would also be critical to attracting greater domestic and international participation.
“Ultimately, it is trust which is our true market infrastructure,” he said.
Mr. Murty also noted that sustained participation by retail investors and domestic institutional investors (DIIs) had helped Indian markets remain resilient amid volatility caused by foreign portfolio investor outflows over the past year.
Echoing the need to deepen capital markets, Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) Chairman Sivasubramanian Ramann called for more efficient mobilisation of long-term savings held by pension funds, provident funds and insurance companies towards infrastructure and corporate financing.
He highlighted the limited availability of long-tenure corporate bonds, particularly 15-year and 35-year instruments, despite growing institutional interest. Infrastructure projects, he said, would require patient capital backed by an appropriate mix of equity and debt.
“Without the right mix of equity and debt, we will never be able to leverage capital effectively. We desperately need infrastructure financing, and in my view, that is only going to come from long-term capital,” Mr. Ramann said.
He also pointed to improving access to IPOs for companies that have established themselves in the unlisted space, saying this was widening corporate funding avenues and making capital markets more accessible to businesses.
