briefs.headline: Anthropic's listing bonanza: Over 5,000 employees become millionaires overnight
briefs.deck: Anthropic's recent IPO significantly increased employee wealth, turning approximately 5,100 staff members into millionaires. The company’s rapid growth has created substantial equity value for both early and current employees. Many employees are witnessing significant financial gains as a result of stock-based compensation. This event marks one of the largest such windfalls in Silicon Valley's…
briefs.bodyText:
Anthropic made a blockbuster debut on Wall Street on Thursday (local time), with its valuation touching $2 trillion and the stock ending its first trading session nearly 17% higher.
But the listing brought an even bigger windfall for the company's employees. Anthropic's remarkable journey from a small artificial intelligence startup to one of the world's most valuable companies has turned nearly its entire workforce into millionaires on paper, with some employees holding fortunes worth hundreds of millions of dollars.
Priced at $83 per share, the IPO has created thousands of paper millionaires, spanning early researchers and engineers to administrative staff who received stock grants as the company expanded. Around 600 employees now have equity holdings worth more than $100 million, while nearly 5,100 staff members have shares valued at over $1 million.
The scale of the employee wealth creation could make Anthropic's listing one of the biggest financial windfalls in Silicon Valley history.
Over 5,000 employees get $1 million
Anthropic had a workforce of 5,300 as of September this year, according to regulatory filings. Data from Hill.com, which tracks private-company shares, shows that around 5,100 employees, or 96% of the total workforce, hold equity worth more than $1 million.
The figures go much higher for a significant section of the staff. Around 2,800 employees, known internally as “Ants”, have stock holdings valued at more than $10 million. Another 600 have crossed the $100 million threshold, placing them in the “centi-millionaire” category.
Andrew Benson, founder and CEO of Hill, told CNN on Thursday that the speed of this wealth creation stood out, particularly given how few employees had left the company. “What’s most surprising here is how quickly this this happened,” Benson said.
He added, “It’s been pretty clear for some time that Anthropic is a rocket ship, and so it definitely discouraged people from leaving because they knew what the opportunity cost of that would be.”
Anthropic's sudden rise
Anthropic's employee wealth boom is closely linked to how quickly the company expanded. Founded in 2021, it had fewer than 1,000 employees at the end of 2024. By September this year, its headcount had reached 5,300.
Stock-based compensation is a familiar feature of Silicon Valley startups, where companies often combine salaries with equity grants because they have limited cash to pay employees. The prospect of an eventual acquisition or IPO can also encourage employees to remain with a company until they can realise the value of their shares.
But Anthropic's experience highlights how much the timing of joining a company can matter when it comes to financial returns.
Benson said employees who joined earlier could end up with significantly larger gains than those who entered the company at a more senior level much later.
As he put it, “being early is more important, in terms of a financial outcome, than being senior … You could be very low on the totem pole, and if you joined in 2023 or 2024, you’re likely to have a significantly better outcome than a senior person who joined earlier this year.”
SpaceX comparison: Anthropic's wealth creation came much faster
The scale of Anthropic's employee windfall can be compared with SpaceX's IPO, which created around 4,400 millionaires from a workforce of 22,000.
However, SpaceX had spent more than two decades as a private company before its blockbuster listing in June. Anthropic, founded in 2021, has reached a similar milestone much earlier in its journey.
The two companies also differ in how their employees are distributed. SpaceX has staff across Texas, California and Florida, while Anthropic's workforce is concentrated in San Francisco.
Employees get an early opportunity to sell shares
Anthropic's IPO also stands apart because it gave non-founder insiders an opportunity to sell part of their holdings from the first day of trading.
Typically, employees at companies going public must wait through a “lockup” period, which generally lasts between three and six months, before they can sell their shares.
Anthropic instead introduced a complex, staggered lockup schedule that allowed non-founder insiders to cash out up to 10% of their shares as soon as trading began. However, it is not known how many employees used this option on Thursday.

briefs.headline: New Air India CEO briefs Noel, Chandra at Gurugram HQ
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI/NEW DELHI: Months after Noel Tata, chairman of Tata Trusts and a director of 
Tata Sons
, questioned the financial performance of 
Air India
, he joined fellow Tata Sons directors on a visit to the airline's Gurugram headquarters and training academy on Thursday.
The visit, organised by Tata Sons and Air India chairman 
N Chandrasekaran
, was part of a broader effort to give directors deeper insight into the airline's operations, transformation programme and turnaround progress. Trusts vice-chairman and Tata Sons director Venu Srinivasan was the only absentee and is learnt to be in Botswana.
Air India's new chief executive, Tewolde Gebremariam outlined the airline's roadmap to profitability, including plans to improve efficiencies, strengthen cost controls and drive greater synergies with Air India Express. Tata Sons directors also visited the airline's operations control centre, housed within the Gurugram campus. The visit came a day ahead of Air India's board meeting on Friday and followed hours of interactions between directors and the airline's senior management team.
Air India has drawn scrutiny from Noel over losses and capital allocation. At Tata Sons' Feb board meeting, Noel raised concerns over the performance of Air India and other newer ventures, leading to the deferment of Chandrasekaran's reappointment as chairman.
On Nov 14, Noel said he did not question "the direction" of Tata Sons' investments but questioned "the delivery" of those initiatives. Following the Feb board meeting, Chandrasekaran initiated a process under which heads of Air India, Tata Digital and Tata Electronics would present their financial and operational plans directly to the Tata Sons board.
He also proposed visits by directors to Air India's Gurugram headquarters, Tata Electronics' semiconductor project at Dholera and Tata Digital's fulfillment and dark-store operations. Former Air India CEO Campbell Wilson, Tata Digital CEO Sajith Sivanandan and Tata Electronics CEO Randhir Thakur subsequently briefed directors on their businesses at Tata Sons board meeting in May. Thursday's visit to Air India's Gurugram facility marks the first board-level operational review under the initiative.
Earlier this month, Tewolde said Air India has "punched below its weight" for too long and is mulling a fresh order for more wide body aircraft to "regain market share from competition (foreign airlines)" as that "business belongs to Air India." While the "short term" poses multiple "challenges", the "long term is a huge opportunity" and the airline could be profitable "very soon" by focusing on cutting costs and boosting revenue and efficiency, he said on Nov 3.

briefs.headline: Piyush Goyal calls for trusted supply chains between India & US
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Commerce and industry minister 
Piyush Goyal
 on Thursday called for building resilient and trusted supply chains between India and the US amid prevailing global uncertainties. This helps countries reduce dependence on one geography, securing supplies of critical goods and strengthening India-US economic and strategic ties, the minister said.
Addressing the Indo-US Economic Summit here, he said huge potential exists between the two countries to enhance economic cooperation, as the US offers capital, technology, and innovation, while India offers skills, talent, manufacturing strength, and competitiveness. Goyal said he would conclude with five calls to action, using the acronym TRUST to outline his suggestions.
"T - the first letter. Let us turn our supply chains into resilient and trusted supply chains. 'R', let us raise our talent together with our friendly and partner countries," he said. The minister suggested increasing collaborations between Indian and US universities. "I am working with some of them to bring them to India," he added.
He said 'S' in the TRUST acronym stands for 'Speak', urging both sides to communicate candidly and openly flag any hurdles or difficulties they face.
He said the final 'T' stood for 'Track', emphasising the need to monitor outcomes and urging the IACC to hold both sides accountable.
India needs about $430 billion in goods and services exports between Nov and March to meet its $1 trillion target for 2026-27, Goyal said, adding that India will have preferential trade access to $85 trillion of global GDP by next year, up from $70 trillion at present, as ongoing trade negotiations add another $15 trillion.

briefs.headline: Expect more coordination among regulators: RBI DG
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: 
RBI
 deputy governor SC Murmu has called attention to overlapping regulatory jurisdictions in India's financial sector, pointing to related-party transactions, mis-selling of insurance and mutual fund products, and cybersecurity as areas requiring coordination among regulators.
Speaking at the Gatekeepers of Governance 2026 event in Mumbai, Murmu said the mandates of financial regulators intersected in several areas, requiring greater coordination to address risks that cut across institutions and markets.
A listed bank, for instance, is subject to RBI's prudential norms and related-party lending guidelines as well as listing regulations governing related-party transactions. "As regulators, our mandates intersect at many points," he said.
The distribution of insurance and mutual fund products by banks is another area of overlap, with mis-selling falling within the jurisdiction of multiple regulators. "Banks distribute insurance and mutual funds, so mis-selling concerns all three regulators," he said.
Cybersecurity presents a similar challenge because an incident at one institution can affect entities overseen by different regulators. Murmu said regulators needed to establish common standards for cyber resilience. 
"A single incident can hit a bank, an insurer, and a market infrastructure institution at once," he said.
He said coordination among regulators would be necessary to address these overlapping responsibilities. "You can expect closer coordination among us," he said. Murmu also said regulation needed to focus on clearly communicating expectations rather than attempting to keep pace with every new development through additional rules.

briefs.headline: Irdai flags conflict in banks, auto cos selling insurance
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Irdai chairman Ajay Seth has called for stronger corporate governance in the insurance sector, citing potential conflicts of interest when lenders sell insurance and automobile dealers combine insurance distribution with vehicle repair services.
He also called for boards to act as the first gatekeepers of governance, drawing on RBI's engagement with bank and NBFC boards. Separately, he questioned whether financial regulators should erect barriers between sectors or allow savings to move towards more efficient managers, while flagging risks from the widespread use of AI in insurance underwriting and claims settlement.
Speaking at the Gatekeepers of Governance 2026 event in Mumbai helmed by former Sebi chief M Damodaran, Seth said business models that had served the industry for decades could also create conflicts of interest. He said boards needed to establish safeguards to ensure these conflicts did not compromise customer interests.
"Some business models have served very well over decades, but that brings in the associated risks in terms of conflict of interest," Seth said. Citing lenders selling insurance and automobile dealers combining insurance distribution with damage repair services, he said, "These are the two different signs of services. 
They have to be kept separately rather than mixing with each other."
Seth said boards had a responsibility to establish safeguards against such conflicts. "The role of the board becomes more important, that what kind of a guardrail it sets to take care that those conflicts of interest do not come in the way of providing the best advice, best service, best product to the customers," he said.
He also called for the insurance sector to strengthen corporate governance by adopting practices followed by RBI in its engagement with banks and NBFCs. He cited RBI's structured interactions with company boards and independent directors as an approach that had helped improve governance across the financial sector.
On the movement of household savings between financial products, Seth questioned whether regulators should create barriers between sectors or facilitate the flow of savings towards more efficient managers. He said changing preferences were reshaping the way savings were managed and called for greater coordination among financial regulators.
Seth also flagged the risks arising from the growing application of artificial intelligence tools in the insurance sector.

briefs.headline: Up to 90% corpus withdrawal allowed in major PF reform
briefs.deck: Wait To Encash In Case Of Job Loss Cut To 2 Months
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Employees Provident Fund Organisation (
EPFO
) on Thursday decided to let retiring members opt for a systematic withdrawal plan (SWP) - giving them the opportunity to withdraw only a part of their corpus and earn interest on the remaining amount. Till now, members had to withdraw the entire corpus within three years of retirement.
Separately, in case of partial withdrawals - a year after mandating that 25% of the corpus must be kept as minimum balance with EPFO - it decided to dilute the rule and allowed members to withdraw 90% of their corpus for three specified categories - essential needs (illness, education, marriage); housing needs; and special circumstances. Besides, it also slashed the waiting period in case of withdrawals made during the period of joblessness to two months, instead of 12 months earlier. "(EPFO) approved the provisions relating to the minimum balance requirement and waiting period for withdrawal, with a view to safeguarding the long-term social security interests of EPF members," the retirement fund body stated.
Under SWP, retiring members can withdraw their accumulated PF savings at regular intervals, such as monthly, quarterly or half-yearly, based on their preference. 
Subscribers will also have the option to stop SWP whenever they want, apart from partial lumpsum withdrawal or only withdrawing the interest earned.
The SWP facility would be entirely voluntary, thus ensuring stable post-retirement income, reducing reinvestment risks and strengthening fund sustainability. The minimum waiting period for making withdrawals under Employee Pension Scheme (EPS), however, remains unchanged at 36 months.
Around 6.3 lakh EPF members aged above 55 years with provident fund accumulations of over Rs 5 lakh are expected to be primary beneficiaries of the proposed SWP framework. In case of the member's death during the payout period, a nominee or dependant will be able to withdraw the remaining balance or continue receiving periodic payments.
TOIreported about this in a frontpage report Thursday.
Vineet Nahata, MD, Power Gilt Treasuries, and member of Central Board of Trustees, said members will now get completely secure fixed income investment avenue with attractive interest earning, that too tax exempt till Rs 2.5 lakh annually. "It is a superior investment alternative compared to bank fixed deposits and mutual funds which are prone to credit risk and market fluctuations," he said.
Additionally, in a move towards achieving universal social security, EPFO approved the introduction of a UAN-linked mechanism for direct voluntary contributions and third-party micro-contributions (such as customer tips), completely independent of traditional employer payroll systems. This will help people in the unorganised sector to accumulate their own PF savings, independent of any employer contributions.
With a view to diversifying EPFO's investment portfolio and generate higher returns for its 30 crore members, the social security organisation also decided to permit investments up to 3% of its fresh annual accretions in eligible alternative investment funds. It can invest up to 5% of its fresh annual accretions in asset-backed and trust-structured investments, according to its pattern of investment. 
Initially, the plan is to channel worker capital through institutional giants such as National Investment and Infrastructure Fund and Sidbi's Startup India Fund of Funds 2.0.
CBT also reviewed proposals for 27 establishments to surrender their EPF exemptions status and four establishments to have their exemption cancelled, transferring corpus of around Rs 6,000 crore, covering 1.5 lakh members, to EPFO's direct administration. Exempted establishments manage PFs on their own in accord with EPFO norms.

briefs.headline: Trump administration approved nearly 9 lakh Nvidia and AMD AI chips for Chinese firms
briefs.deck: In a recent development, shipments of 879,868 AI chips from Nvidia and AMD, destined for Chinese firms linked to the military, have sparked security concerns. Among the companies receiving these shipments are notable players like Tencent and Alibaba. The approvals have prompted congressional representatives to demand tighter regulations. Nvidia emphasized that its licensing review was thorough…
briefs.bodyText:
The US, under Donald Trump's administration, approved the shipment of 879,868 AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD to Chinese companies, which were identified as military-linked by the US department of defense.
According to newly released documents from the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the approvals included Nvidia's sensitive H200 chips and their AMD equivalent. The shipments were cleared through 21 licence applications as of May 11.
Some of China's biggest companies featured on the recipient list. Tencent and its subsidiaries were approved to receive 1.5 lakh chips, followed by Alibaba with 75,000, Baidu with 43,000 and BYD with 4,000.
All four companies are on the defense department's 2026 list of alleged Chinese military companies operating in the US.
The disclosures were made possible by a provision under the Export Control Reform Act, which allowed Rep. Brian Mast, chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, to release details of the licence applications.
The committee said Mast exercised his legislative authority to “publicly reveal export control license application information” concerning Nvidia and AMD's AI chip licences for China.
The revelations prompted criticism from Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the committee's ranking member, who questioned the Trump administration's handling of chip export restrictions.
Accusing the administration of mishandling export controls, Meeks said it “has put our national security and technology edge at risk.”
He also questioned the Bureau of Industry and Security's enforcement of the rules, saying it had failed “to enforce the rules.” He added that “Congress must now conduct rigorous oversight of the administration’s policies.”
Nvidia said the licensing process had involved a lengthy review and that the approvals came with restrictions.
An Nvidia spokesperson told The Hill, “the review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes.”
The company also clarified that receiving licences did not mean shipments were continuing. “Despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China,” the spokesperson added.
AMD also responded to the disclosures, saying it followed the applicable US export control requirements.
“AMD complies with applicable U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations,” the company told The Hill in a statement.
The latest disclosure comes amid earlier scrutiny of the Trump administration's decision to approve Nvidia's H200 chip sales last year.
Mast had led House probes into the administration's approval of the shipments. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had previously argued before federal government officials that selling China the company's third- or fourth-best chips would make the country dependent on US-made infrastructure.

stories.headline: Klaasen keen to tap into Gulf Giants' wealth of T20 experience in ILT20 title bid
stories.deck: Heinrich Klaasen begins a new leadership chapter as Gulf Giants captain in ILT20 Season 5, despite limited captaincy experience across his T20 career. Having learned from leaders such as Albie Morkel, Henry Davids and Faf du Plessis, the South African is keen to draw on his squad's experience while ensuring captaincy does not compromise his aggressive batting approach.
stories.bodyText:
Dubai: Heinrich Klaasen
 has played 311 T20 matches across his 15-year career and led a team in just 48 matches. That's just 15.43% of his career. He's held captaincy duties for South Africa, South Africa A, the Northerns, the Titans, the Spartans and the Seattle Orcas. A year on from that stint in Major League Cricket (MLC) in the USA, the South African has been given the armband by the Gulf Giants in the fifth season of the ILT20.
Curiously, in the Giants squad, 
David Miller
 has more T20 captaincy experience. Ibrahim Zadran, Rahmanullah Gurbaz, Liam Livingstone, Azmatullah Omarzai and Curtis Campher have also captained teams across the regional and franchise T20 circuit. Instead of being bogged down by the presence of so many experienced heads in the squad, Klaasen wants to make all their experience count.
"It's a new tournament for me, new conditions that I'm not used to, but we've got so much experience in our team that I will definitely rely on a lot of our players and a lot of local boys that have got heaps of experience. I'm looking forward to the challenge and we've got an incredible squad and a very talented squad. I can't wait for the full team to arrive so we can have good chats and find our basis of how we want to do things," said Klaasen during an interaction with select media ahead of ILT20 Season 5, which begins on November 21.
The 35-year-old has learned from many skippers along the way. Albie Morkel made the biggest impact, teaching him the art of making subtle field changes while still being aggressive. Henry Davids imparted the skill of forming a bond with a player to get the best out of them. Faf du Plessis, at the international level, brought different things, especially technical thinking on the field.
I need to be free enough to still play the aggressive brand of cricket I normally play, or the normal way I play.
Heinrich Klaasen | Gulf Giants captain
"I was always just shouting at everyone and trying to get the best out of them and realised quickly that the new generation of cricket doesn't work like that," explained Klaasen with a chuckle.
Besides his sense of humour, Klaasen also brings the humility needed in a team sport.
"You will never be old enough and experienced enough to learn all the trades of cricket. That's why I've got heaps of experience in my team that I will rely on. I see the cricket game in a certain direction or a certain way, and other guys see the game differently as well. So it's very important for me to put egos aside and tap into the cricket experience that is in the group and the experience of these conditions and the knowledge of the opposition, so I can use it to my ability," he continued.
Klaasen also brings a lot of firepower to the side. The middle-order batter has scored more than 7,000 runs in T20s while piling up 1,000 runs in 58 T20Is, establishing himself as one of the formidable players in the shortest format.
But it is somewhere between captaincy duties and explosive hitting that he'd need to find perfect cohesion. The Giants are yearning for their first ILT20 title since 2023. After that glorious run and an exit in the second qualifier in 2024, they've finished fifth in the last two seasons and missed out on making the playoffs. In the opening season of the competition in the UAE, the Giants topped the points table before winning a comfortable final against the Desert Vipers. The owners and coach Simon Helmot would expect much of the same from Klaasen & Co.
"The batting aspect shouldn't have anything to do with the captaincy. I think that's where the balance needs to come in. I need to be free enough to still play the aggressive brand of cricket I normally play, or the normal way I play. And then on the field is where the captaincy and my brand has to work a little bit different," Klaasen explained his philosophy as he prepared to play the ILT20 for the first time.
The Gulf Giants will open their ILT20 campaign against the Sharjah Warriorz at the Sharjah Cricket Stadium on Sunday.

stories.headline: World Chess Championship: Worry less, enjoy chess more, Anand’s message to Gukesh
stories.deck: At 20, Gukesh and Sindarov are the youngest participants in a world championship match in chess history
stories.bodyText:
The legendary Viswanathan Anand has advised D. Gukesh to enjoy his chess more as the reigning champion looks to regain form ahead of his world title defence against Uzbek challenger Javokhir Sindarov in Geneva from next week.
At 20, Gukesh and Sindarov are the youngest participants in a world championship match in chess history.
“I have told him that sometimes it's better to let go and just relax, because no amount of worrying is going to fix some things,” Anand told reporters on the sidelines of the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot.
Gukesh's form has dipped considerably since winning the world title, with a string of disappointing results this year pushing him down to 26th in the world rankings with a rating of 2710.
He finished last or joint last at the Prague Masters in March, Norway Chess in June and the Quantbox Chennai Grand Masters in July.
“I've been mentioning it to him for five or six years now. A lot of times I told him, 'When I was 20 or when I was 18, I also worried like you.' But there are some points when it's pointless, and worrying isn't going to improve your performance, so you might as well just enjoy it,” he said.
Gukesh, Arjun Erigaisi, R Praggnanandhaa and his sister R Vaishali are often referred to as 'Vishy's kids', having trained at the
Westbridge Anand Chess Academy set up by the five-time world champion.
While Sindarov is a part of Rustam Kasimdzhanov's Uzbek golden generation.
“First of all, the trend is to get younger. Not only India and Uzbekistan, Turkey as well. Of course there are others, but these seem to be ahead, and the Olympiad seems to confirm them.
“I'm happy with them being called Vishy's kids and all, though I'm more careful about taking credit for all sorts of things. I think the youth trend is very strong.
“Computers play a very, very big part in that, but as always, having somebody with some wisdom or experience tell you how to deal with this or that is useful, and probably Rustam filled that role there and I filled it.”
Anand also said Vaishali will draw confidence from her performance at the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot ahead of her Women's World Championship match against China's Ju Wenjun next year.
The Indian Grandmaster, the lowest-rated player in the field here, produced some impressive results at the event, defeating Wesley So and Hans Niemann in blitz before beating compatriot Arjun Erigaisi in a Fast Classical contest.
“It was a very stern test. Something like the win with Arjun she can take a lot of confidence from.”
Anand, the FIDE Deputy President, said the demanding event would have tested Vaishali and helped her identify areas that needed improvement.
“Playing in an event like this will have tested her in many ways, and that's good for her because when she goes back now, she has concrete things to add to her to-do list.
“Otherwise, a to-do list stays too vague: everything looks clean and done and you can tick your boxes, until suddenly you realize, 'Wait, at the board I froze here and I froze there—let me go over that a bit more.’ It was definitely a tough tournament,” Anand said.

stories.headline: 'Pooran': Digvesh Rathi drops hint on LSG's new captain after Pant trade
stories.deck: Pant led LSG in the 2025 and 2026 IPL seasons after joining the franchise for Rs 27 crore at the IPL 2025 mega auction.
stories.bodyText:
Lucknow Super Giants spinner Digvesh Rathi has hinted that 
Nicholas Pooran
 could take over as the franchise's captain in the 
Indian Premier League
 (IPL). While LSG are yet to announce 
Rishabh Pant
's successor, Rathi named the West Indies batter when asked about the team's new captain.
Pant led LSG in the 2025 and 2026 IPL seasons after joining the franchise for Rs 27 crore at the IPL 2025 mega auction. However, he left the team to join Delhi Capitals in a trade deal in June 2026, leaving LSG with the task of finding a new captain.
Pooran is among the frontrunners for the role. He has been part of LSG since 2023 and was retained for Rs 21 crore ahead of the IPL 2025 mega auction. The left-handed wicketkeeper-batter is also the franchise's highest run-scorer in the IPL.
Rathi's response has added to speculation about Pooran's appointment. In a video that is going viral on social media, the Delhi-born spinner was asked about LSG's new captain during Delhi's recent match in the Syed Mushtaq Ali T20 Trophy. He responded by naming Pooran.
Pooran has experience leading teams in T20 cricket. He previously captained the West Indies in T20Is and has also led MI New York in Major League Cricket and MI Emirates in the International League T20 (ILT20).
Apart from Pooran, LSG could consider Mitchell Marsh, Aiden Markram, Sam Curran and Josh Inglis for the captaincy role. Marsh and Markram currently lead Australia and South Africa in T20Is, respectively. Curran has captained Punjab Kings in the IPL and also guided Desert Vipers to their maiden ILT20 title in 2026.
The England all-rounder joined LSG in a trade deal from Rajasthan Royals ahead of the IPL 2027 retention deadline.

stories.headline: IND vs NZ, 1st Test: Rahul and Jaiswal endure stern test after Nicholls and Phillips take New Zealand to 368
stories.deck: Henry Nicholls stood tall amid New Zealand’s lower-order resistance, extending his unbeaten innings to 175
stories.bodyText:
Henry Nicholls stood tall amid New Zealand’s lower-order resistance, extending his unbeaten innings to 175 (335b, 21x4) as the host was bowled out for 368, 40 minutes before tea on the second day of the first Test against India at Basin Reserve on Friday (November 20, 2026).
K.L. Rahul and Yashasvi Jaiswal then endured a stern test by Matt Henry and Kyle Jamieson, surviving an eventful eight overs to take India to 16 without loss at the break.
Jamieson induced multiple edges from Jaiswal that either fell short or flew over the slip cordon, he was unfortunate in the last over of the session when Phillips dropped an edge at gully.
Rahul was particularly fortunate in the penultimate over before tea when Henry struck him in line with the stumps. New Zealand chose not to review an lbw decision that went in the opener’s favour, leaving India’s vice-captain to survive a potentially costly reprieve. The opening pair, having negotiated the first four overs as maidens, will look to settle in after the break.
The second session, however, belonged to New Zealand, with the last three wickets adding 50 runs to push the total past 350. Prasidh Krishna claimed his first wicket of the innings by trapping Nathan Smith in front, while Jamieson offered brief resistance before falling to Akash Deep’s well-directed short ball.
Jasprit Bumrah then picked up his fourth wicket, sending Matt Henry back to the pavilion, but Nicholls continued to farm the strike and frustrate India. He added 20 crucial runs with last-man Jacob Duffy, including a 14-run over off Bumrah, before Duffy failed to negotiate Anshul Kamboj’s short delivery.
Nicholls’ stubborn resistance ensured New Zealand had a substantial first-innings total to work with, despite India’s early strikes and sustained effort with the ball.

briefs.headline: Anand tells Gukesh to relax ahead of World C'ship: 'Worrying won't fix some things'
briefs.deck: Gukesh Dommaraju is gearing up to defend his World Chess Championship title against Javokhir Sindarov in Geneva. Legendary player Viswanathan Anand has encouraged Gukesh to stay calm and focus, suggesting that stress serves no purpose. Both competitors are backed by chess icons, with Anand mentoring Gukesh and Rustam Kazimdzhanov guiding Sindarov.
briefs.bodyText:
BUDAPEST: In a few days from now, Gukesh Dommaraju will step into a hallowed hall in Geneva to defend his World Chess Championship crown against challenger Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan, and 
Viswanathan Anand
 has advised the Chennai boy to relax.
"I have told him that sometimes it's better to let go and just relax because no amount of worrying is going to fix some things," 
Anand
 said on the sidelines of the Total Chess pilot event here on Thursday. "I have been telling him this for 5-6 years now," the five-time world champion, who has also mentored Gukesh, added.
He agrees that Gukesh has become a lot calmer than he was when he won the title two years ago, but won't take credit for that. "I'm going to give credit to his body. He went from a teenager to 20 and that probably played a bigger part (than my advice)."
Sindarov too is 20 and like Gukesh, he too has been mentored by a legend in the game, Uzbek Grandmaster Rustam Kazimdzhanov. Anand and Rustam are often credited with the rise of chess in India and Uzbekistan with the younger players being referred to as 'Anand or Rustam's children'.
"I'm more careful in taking credit for all sorts of things. I think the youth trend is very strong and computers play a very big part," Anand went on. 
"But somebody with some wisdom or experience telling you this is how you can deal with things is useful."
And of course he is not in favour of players forfeiting dead rubbers, like Magnus Carlsen and a few others did during the course of this tournament. " I wouldn't even have realized that it was possible to do such a thing. It's a game day and I will go and play. I would have complained, but I wouldn't have done this," he said. 
He feels there is a gap in the rules and some players are taking advantage of it. " Those rules are something we'll have to tighten."
Talking about Total Chess, Anand feels it's a fascinating idea. "It allows us to experiment with a couple of things, one is to see how much faster you can make Classic. At the same time, combining disciplines in a single day is a very interesting idea. And this gives us the chance to test all that."
(The writer is in Budapest on an invitation from Total Chess)

briefs.headline: IPL has fast-tracked New Zealand cricket’s rise: Ross Taylor
briefs.deck: Ross Taylor provided his observations on the ongoing Test match between India and New Zealand in Wellington. He praised India for their performance and highlighted their bowlers' effectiveness. Taylor noted the cultural evolution within New Zealand cricket thanks to world-class players and experiences in events like the IPL. He emphasised the importance of transitioning to younger players as…
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Ross Talyor has been keenly watching the first Test match between India and New Zealand which began on Thursday at Wellington.
"I think India did well. five for 70, I think they would have found they were in a good position. Henry Nicholls, obviously India have got the new ball, the second new ball tomorrow. And they'll be wanting to take some early wickets. I thought (Jasprit) Bumrah bowled outstandingly well. And it wasn't as green as it normally is in Wellington. I think it browned off pretty quickly after lunch. So I'm sure the Indian batters will want to get through that new ball tomorrow. And if they can do that, we'll look forward to batting on a flat wicket," former New Zealand batter RossTaylor told TOI on Thursday in an exclusive interview at the ProWine event here at the Jio Convention Centre Centre on Thursday.
Talking about the New Zealand cricket team's transformation over the last two decades, Taylor said, "From here, I think it's probably a good summation of where we were as a team. And where we are. Today is chalk and cheese from that. We've got some world-class players now. The likes of (Daniel) Vettori, (Bendon) McCullum, (Tim) Southee, (Trent) Bolt, (Kane) Williamson. I think when you have world-class players on your team, you bring everyone else with you.
 And I think the standards have gone up. And I think probably the 
IPL
 has played a part in that too in having New Zealand players learn and rub shoulders with the best players in the world has, I think, fast-tracked their learning as well."
What has been the biggest cultural shift in New Zealand cricket during his playing career you are tempted to ask Taylor. "I think when you have world-class players, the other players have to lift. I think the culture has been great. And I think the.continuation of the team has just got better and better," he said.
The Blacks Caps have earned a reputation for consistency and humility under 
Kane Williamson
. How much of that culture was built over the years by players like yourself, Ben McCullum and Daniel Vittori? “I think you'd have to ask the other players that. I think New Zealand, as nature, are pretty reserved and humble people. We want to go out there and play hard cricket, but there's still a way to play hard cricket, but play in the spirit of the game as well,” Taylor said.
Does he think New Zealand has maximized its talent pool or there's still untapped potential in the system? "Yes, I think probably a bit of both. I think the team is growing quickly. We've got some good young players coming through. There's always a transition period and the players are getting older, so I think the New Zealand team needs to get a few more youngsters in. Ratchin's (Ravindra) come in and had success, but hopefully we can get some other players. I think we've got some good bowlers coming through, but hopefully some young batters can come through in the next couple of years,” said
How challenging has it been for New Zealand to manage the transition as senior players retire? “That's what I mean. I think that's going to be the key going forward. Just the way the international schedule works, the World Cup plays a big part, so those senior players like to work towards World Cups and quite often retire after that. Once the next World Cup comes around, I think it's a time for New Zealand cricket and probably a lot of other countries to rebuild their teams,” felt Taylor, at Pro Wine 2026 here on Thursday.
Having played alongside former New Zealand captain Kane Williamson for so long, the one quality people outside the dressing room don't fully appreciate, according to Tayor is, "I think he's a great cricketer and a world-class person, and that shows on the cricket field, but that is who he is. I think a lot of players are different from what they are on the field, is what you see from Kane is what you get from him.”
Talking about how he was going about his business of Pro Wines, Taylor said, "It's good to be here at Pro Wines Mumbai as an ambassador for the New Zealand pavilion. If you would have said to me when I retired a few years ago that I'd be in the wine industry, I would have said absolutely no chance. But it's been great to be here and obviously with the New Zealand Free Trade Agreement with India, I think it's a good chance for the two countries that we have strong relationships in a sporting context, but bringing it together in a business capacity will just keep going from strength to strength.
”
Talking about what separates 
Virat Kohli
 from other modern greats in the ODI format, Taylor said, "They'll (Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli) will be there at that World Cup. They're still fit as ever and just their catches that they took in that series, they might have not scored the amount of runs that they would have liked, their athleticism,till there at and 40 and I'm sure for the Indian crowd and, going out there and watching them for their last time, which I hope it's not their last time, but obviously it's getting towards the end of their career and for all cricket fans around the world, hopefully they can play for a bit longer," Taylor concluded.

briefs.headline: 50/4 and a lot of heat: How Akash Deep sparked India's turnaround on Day 2
briefs.deck: India endured a frustrating morning as Henry Nicholls and Glenn Phillips extended their sixth-wicket partnership to 216, but Akash Deep's dismissal of Phillips sparked a turnaround. India struck quickly thereafter, taking New Zealand's last four wickets for just 30 runs to bowl them out for 368. The visitors' post-Lunch response offered relief after a prolonged period of resistance.
briefs.bodyText:
Wellington: The Basin Reserve pitch blended with the outfield in its lushness when both India and New Zealand were putting the finishing touches to their preparations. It had a considerable tinge on the opening day too, but as the players took the field for the second day, the surface started turning brown as the 15mm grass cover took on a burnt look on another sunny morning. The handful of trees circling the ground remained still as the notorious Welly Wind stayed at bay, suggesting another day of chasing leather for the 
Indian cricket team
.
The visitors tried a few different things from the first delivery, hoping to break the frustrating 216-run partnership between 
Henry Nicholls
 and 
Glenn Phillips
 for the sixth wicket. Jasprit Bumrah changed ends, and Prasidh Krishna shared the second new ball with him. The pitch, however, had now lost its opening-day morning sting and looked rather comfortable for batting. The experiment didn't last long as Prasidh continued to bowl erratic lines, and Bumrah couldn't find the rhythm he enjoyed when bowling from the scoreboard end.
India sought wickets, but both Nicholls and Phillips looked rock-solid until Akash Deep produced a peach to dismiss Phillips shortly after he scored a brilliant hundred. Angled in, shaping away and hitting the top of the stumps is every fast bowler's delight, and Akash was pumped. 
The moment lifted the Indian team, which had been very flat during the mammoth stand, and they had their tails up for the remainder of the innings.
Akash looked very good, and Bumrah continued doing Bumrah things as India wasted very little time picking up the remaining four wickets. The lower order and the tail have been India's nemesis in the ongoing World Test Championship (WTC) cycle, but that wasn't the case on Friday. The last four wickets added just 30 runs, and New Zealand collapsed from 318/6 to 368 all out.
On either side of the 216-run stand between Nicholls and Phillips, India can be pleased with their efforts of 70/5 and 50/4. Had India found a way through when the left-right combination kept them wicketless for over five hours, it could well have been a different story for the visitors. Except for the dropped catch late on the opening day, Nicholls looked in absolute control during his unbeaten 175 off 335 balls.
The left-hander enjoyed a very strong control percentage and improved his average at this venue to 91.5. He had in-form Phillips for company for most of his innings, and the right-hander became only the second player to hit hundreds across formats against the same team in a single year. Rohit Sharma achieved the rare feat back in 2017 against Sri Lanka.
New Zealand have 368 on the board, and India will be mighty pleased with how they responded after the hosts' defiance in the morning session. If not for some disciplined bowling post-Lunch, it could have been much worse for Shubman Gill & Co. Over to the batters now.

briefs.headline: Kimi Antonelli - A new face for a new era
briefs.deck: Mercedes team boss punted on the Italian and backed him through a bruising rookie year, a barrage of doubts and a few departing sponsors. But he never once wavered in his belief. The youngest champion in F1 history has repaid that faith, and silenced the critics along the way
briefs.bodyText:
Some nights, a whole country stops and looks at glowing screens, big and small. When people speak of the moon landing, they remember where they were. After this weekend, Italy will remember where it was too. A nation that lives and breathes motorsport sat glued to the television as Kimi Antonelli became the youngest champion in Formula One history.
He is not the first Italian to wear the crown, but he is the first to win it in front of a nation watching together. Alberto Ascari, the last Italian champion, was crowned on August 23, 1953, a few months before the country’s first nationwide television broadcast on January 3, 1954.
The wait took 73 years. The moment, when it came, belonged to everyone.
At the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez in Mexico City, Antonelli needed only two points. He took a podium instead. He finished third, behind Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton, and crossed the line in tears. At 20 years and 68 days, he beat Sebastian Vettel’s record, set at 23 years and 134 days, by more than three years.
Vettel was among the first to send congratulations.

briefs.headline: Just second batter in history! Phillips equals Rohit's rare feat with century
briefs.deck: He is the second player overall to score a century in Tests, ODIs and T20Is against the same opponent in a calendar year.
briefs.bodyText:
New Zealand batter 
Glenn Phillips
 became the first player to score centuries in all three formats of international cricket against India in the same calendar year. He achieved the milestone on Day 2 of the first Test at the Basin Reserve in Wellington on Friday.
Phillips completed his century in the first innings of the ongoing Test, having already scored hundreds against India in ODIs and T20Is earlier this year. He scored 106 in the ODI at Indore on January 18 before hitting 107 off 49 balls in the T20I at Auckland on October 30.
He is the second player overall to score a century in Tests, ODIs and T20Is against the same opponent in a calendar year. Former India captain 
Rohit Sharma
 was the first to achieve the feat, scoring centuries against Sri Lanka in all three formats in 2017.
Phillips also became the first New Zealand batter to score centuries against the same opponent across all three formats. Batting at No. 7 in the first innings of the Wellington Test, he took 194 deliveries to reach the three-figure mark.
Hundreds against a team in all three formats in a calendar year
- Rohit Sharma vs Sri Lanka in 2017
- Glenn Phillips vs India in 2026
Overall, Phillips is the third player, after Australia's Shane Watson and West Indies batter Shai Hope, to score centuries against India in all three international formats.
Phillips was eventually dismissed for 118 when Akash Deep bowled him in the 94th over. The India seamer beat the batter with a delivery that moved away and hit the top of the off stump.
Phillips has now scored centuries in consecutive Tests, having made exactly 100 in New Zealand's 253-run win over England at The Oval in June. He has also scored centuries for New Zealand in all three formats.
His dismissal brought an end to a 216-run partnership with Henry Nicholls, which began in the 29th over, shortly after lunch on Day 1.
Nicholls continued New Zealand's innings after the break and reached his 150 shortly after lunch on Day 2. At the time of writing, New Zealand were 348/8 after 116 overs.

briefs.headline: De Villiers calls Khawaja 'biggest traitor' as sandpaper row explodes
briefs.deck: The controversy resurfaced after Cameron Bancroft released a 4,000-word statement in which he made claims about his former teammates, including Cummins.
briefs.bodyText:
Usman Khawaja
 has been called the “biggest traitor ever seen” by former South Africa captain 
Fanie de Villiers
 as the controversy surrounding Australia's ball-tampering scandal during the 2018 tour of South Africa continues to escalate.
The latest developments have brought fresh scrutiny on several members of the Australian team, including Test captain 
Pat Cummins
. The controversy resurfaced after Cameron Bancroft released a 4,000-word statement in which he made claims about his former teammates, including Cummins.
While Cummins has faced calls to step down as Test captain, there has also been pressure on former coach Lehmann. Cricket Australia (CA) has announced that it will set up an independent forum where anyone involved can share information about the team's use of sandpaper to tamper the ball during the 2018 tour of South Africa.
Khawaja has faced questions over why he waited eight years to say that the entire squad should take collective responsibility for the incident. Former Australia players Matthew Hayden and Ian Healy have also criticised him for discussing the matter publicly.
De Villiers went further, questioning Khawaja's decision to bring the issue back into the public domain.
“I want to go on record saying that Khawaja is probably the biggest traitor that I’ve ever seen in cricket that I’ve read in books and in cricket that I’ve seen over my last 40-50 years of watching the game,” he told 91.3 SportFM.
“He’s broken every single code of conduct that one can think of. He’s sold out his players, fellow players."
“This is not about right or wrong. The wrong has already been handled. It’s already been part of Australian cricket and it’s sad that it’s happened. But this guy has brought everything to the fore again. He’s brought Australian cricket into disrepute all over again. Breaking down of friendships. The code of conduct one has within the team," the former South African cricketer said.
“He’s done everything wrong that one can think of."
Mitchell Johnson believes Cummins may have to step down
Former Australia fast bowler Mitchell Johnson believes Cummins could struggle to continue as Test captain following the claims made by Bancroft and Khawaja. He also questioned whether the Australia skipper's public image could survive the controversy.
Writing in a column for The West Australian, Johnson referred to his previous public disagreements with Cummins and said he believed Bancroft's account of the events.
“I believe Bancroft’s account. It comes across as real and I could feel the words as he was saying them. He came across as himself and he has nothing to lose now. It also lines up with the most detailed accounts we’ve heard from other players,” Johnson wrote.
Johnson said Cummins would come under pressure to step down, despite having stood by his earlier version of events.
“The pressure on Cummins is now immense. I think he will still try to stand by what he has said and his statement with all of the bowlers back in 2021.
“But I think the public pressure for Cummins to stand down as Test captain now will be too much. I just can’t see how his captaincy and personal brand survives this.
“CA needs to do more than a safe-space forum. It’s owed to the fans, and they’ve had enough, like many of us. The investigation failed at the one thing it was meant to do, end this eight years ago with the right outcome. We want the truth, we want answers. But we also wish we had moved on all that time ago.”

briefs.headline: IND vs NZ, 1st Test: Jaiswal, KL Rahul see off new ball threat to bring up 100-run stand
briefs.bodyText:
Jacob Duffy to KL Rahul, 2 runs, played towards covers.
Jacob Duffy to KL Rahul, Fuller in length, on off, angling ni, KL Rahul blocks it out solidly.
Matt Henry to KL Rahul, Just short of a length and on off, KL Rahul dabs it through point for a run.
Tap to make your prediction
Matt Henry to KL Rahul, On a length and on middle, KL Rahul tucks it to short mid-wicket.
Matt Henry to Yashasvi Jaiswal, Full again and on off, Yashasvi Jaiswal drives it towards mid off for a single.
Matt Henry to Yashasvi Jaiswal, Goes fuller and on off, Yashasvi Jaiswal drills it towards mid off.
Matt Henry to Yashasvi Jaiswal, Back of a length and on off, nips back in, Yashasvi Jaiswal tries to cut again but this is too close to his body. He ends up chopping it down to the off side.
Matt Henry to Yashasvi Jaiswal, FOUR! Fine shot! Short of a length and outside off. Yashasvi Jaiswal uses the width on offer and cuts it away through point for a boundary.
Jacob Duffy to Yashasvi Jaiswal, Hits the deck hard, on middle and leg, Yashasvi Jaiswal clips it through square leg for a single.
Jacob Duffy to Yashasvi Jaiswal, Good length and on off, Yashasvi Jaiswal pats it in front of short cover.
Jacob Duffy to Yashasvi Jaiswal, Bangs in a bouncer now, on middle, Yashasvi Jaiswal ducks under it.
Jacob Duffy to Yashasvi Jaiswal, FOUR! Much more in control! A half-volley, on off. Yashasvi Jaiswal leans into his drive and creams it through covers for another boundary.
Jacob Duffy to Yashasvi Jaiswal, FOUR! A bit streaky! Lands this back of a length and around off. Yashasvi Jaiswal opens the bat face to steer it away, but gets it off the outer half of the bat through the slip cordon for a boundary.
Jacob Duffy to Yashasvi Jaiswal, Fuller in length and on middle, Yashasvi Jaiswal gets behind the line of it and blocks it out.
Nathan Smith to Yashasvi Jaiswal, Hits the deck hard, around off, Yashasvi Jaiswal rides the bounce and punches it through covers for three runs.
Nathan Smith to Yashasvi Jaiswal, Back of a length and on off, Yashasvi Jaiswal guides it off the outer half of the bat through point for a brace.
Nathan Smith to Yashasvi Jaiswal, FOUR! Cheeky! Nathan Smith bangs this into the pitch, on middle. Yashasvi Jaiswal bends his back to sway away from it and upper-cuts it late over the keeper's head for a boundary. 100 up or India!
Nathan Smith to Yashasvi Jaiswal, Hard length and on middle, angling in again. Yashasvi Jaiswal gets half-forward to defend but gets an inside edge onto his pads. There is a big shout for LBW, but it's turned down. Smith singnals to his captain that there is bat involved.
Nathan Smith to KL Rahul, Good length and on middle, angling in, KL Rahul tucks it towards mid-wicket for a single.
Nathan Smith to KL Rahul, On a length and on off, KL Rahul opens the bat face and steers it towards backward point.
DRINKS! The Indian openers have given them a fantastic start, reducing the trail to 271 runs. Yashasvi Jaiswal has already brought up his fifty, while KL Rahul has also looked solid. Things could have been different had New Zealand taken their chances early on. Matt Henry and Kyle Jamieson have created a few opportunities, but Jacob Duffy has been pretty expensive alongside Nathan Smith, and they will have to pull it together if they want to pick up wickets before the end of day's play...
Jacob Duffy to Yashasvi Jaiswal, On a good length, angled across off. Jaiswal stays back, gets a bit squared up and nudges it down to gully.
Jacob Duffy to Yashasvi Jaiswal, FOUR! That's poor from Duffy, and he's bowling too many bad balls at the moment. Shortish length, drifted down the leg side. Jaiswal hops up a bit and just tickles it off the pads, getting it down to fine leg for a third boundary of the over.
Jacob Duffy to Yashasvi Jaiswal, A well-directed bumper this time, over middle stump, and Jaiswal ducks under it well.
Jacob Duffy to Yashasvi Jaiswal, A length ball around off, Jaiswal gets onto the front foot and blocks it to the off side.
Jacob Duffy to Yashasvi Jaiswal, FOUR! Well, that's an ugly shot from Jaiswal, but he gets the result in his favour. Hard length over middle and off, Jaiswal has a wild slog across the line but gets an outside edge that flies over the slip cordon and races away to the fence.
Jacob Duffy to Yashasvi Jaiswal, FOUR! Yashasvi Jaiswal has been prolific down the ground, and he brings up his 14th Test FIFTY with a gorgeous shot. Full of a good length, around middle. Jaiswal just leans on and punches it on the up, nailing it straight down the ground for a boundary.
Nathan Smith to KL Rahul, Good-length delivery outside off, rushing the batter off the deck again. Rahul stays back and waits well before steering it to point.
Nathan Smith to KL Rahul, Good length, straighter in line and slanting back in. Rahul plays it late, dabbing it down in front of mid-wicket.
Nathan Smith to KL Rahul, Hard length, sliding it into the pads, and this is tucked away to square leg.
Nathan Smith to KL Rahul, Slightly fuller now and on off, rushing the batter off the deck. Rahul goes back and across to the off side, defending it to the on side. Smith has overstepped once again, and it will be a NO Ball.
Nathan Smith to KL Rahul, Just back of a length, over off and middle. Rahul stays back and blocks it off.
Nathan Smith to Yashasvi Jaiswal, Similar line and length to the previous ball, albeit a bit fuller and straighter. Jaiswal leans on and flicks it away through mid-wicket. The fielder at deep square leg runs around a long way to his right and cuts it off. The batters easily come back for the third run.
Nathan Smith to Yashasvi Jaiswal, Pitched up on off and middle, angling back in. Jaiswal is drawn into the drive, hitting it against the angle, and slices it to cover-point.
Kyle Jamieson to KL Rahul, Good length on off, slanting back in. Rahul covers the line well and keeps it out. Still, no breakthrough for the KIwis, and the two Indian batters are scoring at a pretty decent rate right now.
Kyle Jamieson to KL Rahul, Pitched up fuller and outside off, extra lift off the deck, but that's after leaving the batter. Rahul hops past the off stump and shoulders arms.
Kyle Jamieson to KL Rahul, Nagging length on off, angling back into the front pad. Rahul opts to play it off the back foot and gets an inside edge that rolls down to fine leg. The fielder over there runs to his right and slides in to cut it off. Two taken.
Kyle Jamieson to KL Rahul, Pitched much fuller and on off stump, Rahul gets nicely forward and jams it back to the bowler.
Kyle Jamieson to KL Rahul, Good length on off, blocked off by Rahul.
Kyle Jamieson to KL Rahul, Good length around off, the ball bounces steeply and Rahul does well to just cushion it off the higher part of the blade. The ball goes toward gully, where there is a misfield and Rahul wants the single, but Jaiswal rightly sends him back.
Nathan Smith to Yashasvi Jaiswal, A bit of aggression shown here by Nathan Smith. Pitched full and straight, Jaiswal punches it into the deck and to the left of the bowler, who gets around, picks the ball and throws it back wide of the stumps at the keeper's end.
Nathan Smith to KL Rahul, Good running. Length ball at the stumps, Rahul leans on halfway and drops it into the leg side, scampering through for the single.
Nathan Smith to KL Rahul, Pitched up at the stumps, on off and middle, and kept out by Rahul. Smith has overstepped, and the umpire signals a No Ball.
Nathan Smith to KL Rahul, Good-length delivery, angling in from the fifth-stump line, with some extra carry as well. Rahul simply shoulders arms at it.
Nathan Smith to KL Rahul, Good length, in and around off stump. Rahul gets forward to defend.
Nathan Smith to KL Rahul, FOUR! Down the wrong line, and it will be yet another boundary for India. Fractionally short, slipping it down leg, and Rahul just tucks it off the legs and the ball trickles away into the fine leg fence.
Nathan Smith to KL Rahul, Full of a good length, outside off and just nipping back in a bit. Rahul hops past the off stump to cover the line and leaves it alone.
Kyle Jamieson to Yashasvi Jaiswal, FOUR! Overpitched and punished! Too full and wide, Yashasvi Jaiswal leans across and clatters the drive past cover for a boundary. Jaiswal is now into the 40s and looking far more relaxed.
Kyle Jamieson to KL Rahul, Dug in well short over middle, Rahul gets on top of the bounce and plays a controlled hook shot down to deep square leg, picking up a single.
Kyle Jamieson to KL Rahul, Rahul wanted a quick single there, but Jaiswal sent him back. Back of a length, in and around off, Rahul stays back, playing it late and nudging it wide of point.
